en: Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya, Volume One.
Composed by Bodhisattva Maitreya;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen Dynasty.
I pay homage to the son of noble conduct, who was able to compose this correct treatise and expound it for our sake;
I shall now clarify its meaning. First, the establishment of the body of the treatise.
Characteristics, obscurations, and reality; The cultivation of the path of remedies;
Abiding in practice and attaining the fruit— Such are the seven meanings of the Unsurpassed Vehicle as explained in this treatise.
What are the seven? First, characteristics;
second, hindrances; third, reality; fourth, the cultivation of remedies; fifth, dwelling in cultivation; sixth, attaining the fruit; and seventh, the Unsurpassed Vehicle.
Now, based on their characteristics, this verse is spoken:
False discrimination exists; therein, duality does not exist.
Within it, there is only emptiness; and within this, that also exists.
In this context, "unreal imagination" (abhūtaparikalpa) refers to the imagination of the grasper and the grasped.
"Existence" means that there is only imagination.
"Therein" refers to unreal imagination.
"Non-duality" means that these two—the grasper and the grasped—are eternally non-existent.
"Within that" refers to within conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
"Only emptiness exists" means that this very conceptual construction is devoid of both the grasper and the grasped.
"Only that which is empty of this" refers to the emptiness of the grasper and the grasped.
"There is also that" refers to the existence of false conceptualization.
If a phenomenon is absent from a particular location, that location is said to be empty of that phenomenon; what remains there is called "existent."
If one knows in this way, there will be no inversion regarding the wisdom of the characteristic of emptiness.
Next, a verse is spoken:
"Therefore it is said that all phenomena are neither empty nor non-empty."
Existence, non-existence, and existence because [of the former]—this is called the meaning of the Middle Way.
"All phenomena" refers to the conditioned as false conceptualization and the unconditioned as emptiness.
"It is not empty" means that it exists by virtue of emptiness and false discrimination (*vikalpa*).
"It is not non-empty" means that it exists by virtue of the grasper and the grasped.
"It exists" means that false discrimination exists.
"Non-existence" refers to the absence of both the grasping subject and the grasped object.
"And existence" refers to the fact that within false appearances there is true emptiness, and within true emptiness there is also false conceptualization.
That which is called the meaning of the Middle Way refers to the fact that all dharmas are neither exclusively empty nor exclusively non-empty.
Such passages do not contradict the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras; as it is said in the sutras:
"All dharmas are neither empty nor non-empty."
Thus, having already explained that false discrimination possesses both aspects and lacks aspects, we shall now explain its essential nature. Therefore, a verse is spoken:
"Objects, sense organs, self, and consciousness— the fundamental consciousness arises appearing as these."
But consciousness exists only because of that [object]; since that object is non-existent, consciousness is non-existent.
That which resembles the object refers to the fundamental consciousness manifesting as something similar to form and so forth.
That which resembles the sense faculties refers to the consciousness manifesting as the five sense faculties within one's own or another's continuum.
"Resembling the self" refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because it is associated with the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and so forth.
"Resembling consciousness" refers to the six types of consciousness.
"Fundamental consciousness" refers to the *ālayavijñāna*.
"Arising as resembling them" means appearing similar to the four objects, such as external forms and so forth.
"Only consciousness exists" means that there is only the deluded consciousness.
"Those [objects] do not exist" means that the four objects do not exist.

Why is this? Because it is a consciousness of form that resembles objects and resembles sense organs rather than being their actual reality; and because it manifests as a self and as consciousness in a manner that does not accord with the external realm.
As for the statement "because those do not exist, consciousness does not exist," it means that since the objects do not exist, consciousness is likewise non-existent.
These four kinds of objects apprehended by consciousness—namely, the sense-fields, the sense-faculties, the self, and consciousness—are comprised of no real substance or characteristic.
Since that which is apprehended does not exist, the deluded consciousness that apprehends it is likewise non-existent.
Having thus explained the nature and characteristics [of consciousness], we shall now clarify its meaning; therefore, a verse is spoken:
"The nature of deluded consciousness is false; it is by virtue of this meaning that [the distinction] is established."
Because they are neither truly existent nor non-existent, liberation is attained by extinguishing them.
As for how the nature of deluded consciousness as being false and illusory is established by this principle: it means that all that belongs to the world is merely deluded consciousness.
Why is this disordered consciousness called false?
It is because its objects are unreal and its nature is distracted.
That they are not truly existent means that although they appear as four things, those four things are eternally non-existent.
Regarding the phrase "not because it is non-existent in reality," this means that it is not the case that everything is eternally non-existent, since it arises from a deluded consciousness.
Why, then, do you not allow that deluded consciousness is eternally non-existent?
Therefore, the verse says:
Because of the cessation of those [defilements], there is liberation.

If one were to cling to the view that they are eternally non-existent, then neither bondage nor liberation would be established; thus, one would give rise to false views by repudiating both the pure and impure categories.
Having thus explained the essential characteristics of the false,
we shall now explain the characteristics of its subsumption.
If it is said that [all things] are merely false, how can they subsume the three natures?
Therefore, it is said in verse:
The imagined, the dependent, and the perfected—these are the three natures.
They are taught by virtue of objects, the deluded consciousness, And the non-existence of both.
The nature of discrimination refers to the six sense objects, which are eternally unobtainable, like flowers in the sky.
The nature of dependence refers to nothing but the deluded consciousness; because its existence is not real, it is like a magical illusion.
Reality (tattva) refers to the non-existence of both the grasper and the grasped; because it is the true existence of non-existence, it is like space.
Having thus explained the characteristics subsumed under the false, [the following is said:]
Now, the characteristics of the skillful means for entering into the falsity of non-existence shall be explained; therefore, a verse is spoken:
"Because one relies upon consciousness-only, The meaning that objects lack intrinsic nature is established;
Since external objects have no substance, The fundamental consciousness does not arise."

The entire triple world consists of nothing but consciousness; based on this principle, it is definitively established that external objects have no substantial nature whatsoever, and this wisdom is thereby accomplished.

Because the objective referent lacks any substantial entity, the subjective consciousness that takes it as its object cannot arise either. By this expedient means, one enters into the state where both the grasped and the grasper are non-existent.
Therefore, although consciousness is established, its intrinsic nature is not that of consciousness.
Since the various objects of cognition have no substantial essence, the nature of consciousness cannot be established through reasoning.
Regarding "non-cognition" and "cognition," the *Sūtra* manuscript states: "One should know that non-cognition is cognition; by virtue of this meaning, they are equal.
As for "non-cognition," because it is not established by way of its own nature (*svabhāva*), it is therefore not cognition.
This dharma is truly of a nature that is non-existent, yet it can manifest as if it were real objects; therefore, it is called "consciousness.
Having thus explained the characteristics of the skillful means for entering into the false and non-existent.
Now, in order to clarify the general characteristics of the false and illusory, a verse is spoken:

"As for the general categories of the false and illusory, they consist of the mind and mental factors of the three realms. [Note: The commentary states that the edition collated by Sū (疏) lacks the character "not" (不).]
Regarding "falsehood" (mṛṣā): if established in terms of the realms (dhātu), it refers to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
If established in terms of birth (upapatti), it refers to the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta), which constitute the general characteristic of their category.
Having explained the general characteristics, the specific characteristics shall now be explained:
Only consciousness of objects is called "mind" (*citta*); its distinctions are called "mental factors" (*caitasika*).

The mind (citta) merely cognizes the general characteristics (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) of objects; when it cognizes the specific characteristics (viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa) of objects, it is called mental factors (caitasika-dharma), namely feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), formations (saṃskāra), and so forth.
Having thus explained the general and specific characteristics, [the text continues].
Next, the characteristics of arising are revealed:
the first is called the object-condition consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*);
the second is the active consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), which undergoes discrimination regarding objects; and that which induces the formations is called the mental factors (*caitta*).
The "conditioning consciousness" refers to the ālayavijñāna, because it serves as the causal condition for the arising of the other consciousnesses.
The "functioning consciousness" refers to that which arises toward objects based on the ālayavijñāna; this is termed the functioning consciousness.
Regarding "feeling toward objects" (*viṣaya-vedanā*): this refers to the experiencing of the suffering and so forth of objects, which is termed the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*).
Regarding "discrimination": this refers to the discernment of the distinctions among objects, which is termed the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

The "formations" (saṃskāra) are those factors that cause the mind to relinquish one thing and grasp another—namely, desire, volition, attention, and so forth—and these are called the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha).
Likewise, sensation and the others are called mental factors (caitasika-dharma).
Having explained the characteristic of origination, the characteristic of false defilement shall now be explained; thus, a verse is spoken:
Concealment and establishment, Leading and maintaining.
The three parts are perfected: experiencing, contact, and drawing forth;
Clinging and manifestation—because they are suffering, they afflict the world.
There are three kinds and two kinds of difficulties, And seven more arising from falsehood.
"Concealment" refers to ignorance, because it is able to obstruct the seeing of reality as it is.
"Establishment" refers to the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), because they are able to establish karma by perfuming the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Regarding "leading": because the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) enable sentient beings to proceed toward the place of rebirth.
Regarding "sustaining": this refers to how form (*rūpa*) sustains the five aggregates of one's own body.
"Perfection" means that [contact] is able to produce and grow by means of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
"Established through three factors" means that various contacts are established in dependence upon the sense faculty (*indriya*), the object (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
"Experiencing contact" refers to [the stage] where pleasure, pain, and so forth cause benefit or harm.
"Projecting" refers to [the stage] where craving enables karma to project a future birth.
"Attachment" refers to [the stage] where the four graspings cause the various consciousnesses to become defiled and attached to the four bases, such as desire, thereby following along toward rebirth.
"Manifestation" refers to existence through karma; that is, the various karmas already performed tend toward rebirth in order to yield their retribution.
"Suffering" refers to birth, old age, and death.
"Afflicting the world" means that the three realms are oppressed by everything from ignorance through old age and death, and thus constantly experience suffering and hardship.
Regarding the "three kinds and two kinds of hardships," which are also sevenfold due to falsehood: the three kinds of hardships refer to afflictions (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and birth (*jāti*).
The obstacles of affliction refer to ignorance, craving, and grasping.
The obstacles of karma refer to volitional formations and becoming.
The "difficulties regarding birth" refers to the remaining seven parts.
The two kinds of difficulties refer to cause and effect.
The "difficulty regarding cause" refers to the divisions of afflictions and karma.
The "difficulties regarding the fruit" refers to the remaining factors.
The "seven difficulties" refer to seven kinds of causes:
first, the cause of inversion, which is ignorance (*avidyā*).
Second is the cause of attraction, which refers to the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
Third is the cause of leading, which refers to the primary consciousness and the two types of mental consciousness.
Fourth is the cause of appropriation, which refers to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Fifth is the cause of enjoyment, namely contact (*sparśa*) and sensation (*vedanā*).
Sixth is the cause of elicitation, namely craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*).
Seventh is the cause of dread, namely birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
Regarding "arising from the false": such sufferings and difficulties arise from the false.

There are nine aspects to the meaning of the accumulation of the false, namely: the aspect of existence, the aspect of non-existence, the aspect of self-characteristic, the aspect of inclusion, the aspect of entering non-existence, the aspect of skillful means, the aspect of differentiation, the aspect of various names, the aspect of the conditions for arising, and the aspect of defilement; these meanings manifest before one.
Having explained the false, one should now explain the skillful means for revealing the meaning of emptiness. Because they correspond to one another, the verse says:
The essence, the characteristics, and the various names; Their meanings and their conceptualizations;
The principles by which they are established— One should know that the brief explanation of emptiness is thus.
How should the characteristic of emptiness be understood?
The verse says:
Non-duality, and the existence of this non-existence—these two are called the characteristic of emptiness.
Therefore, it is neither existent nor non-existent, neither different nor identical.
"The absence of duality" means the absence of both the grasped object and the grasping subject.
"The existence of this absence" means that while the grasped object exists, the grasping subject is absent.
Regarding these two being called the "characteristic of emptiness": it refers to non-existence and existence-and-non-existence; these are called the characteristic of emptiness.
This reveals that true emptiness has no dual characteristics; this dharma takes the absence of both as its nature, such that it cannot be said to exist and cannot be said not to exist.
Why is it not existent?
Because these two do not exist.
Why is it not non-existent?
Because these two do not exist,
the verse says:
"Neither existent nor non-existent— this is called the characteristic of true emptiness."
"Neither different nor identical" means that it does not have a characteristic different from false conceptualization, nor does it have a characteristic identical to it.

If they were different, it would mean that the dharma-nature is different from the dharma; this is not the case, just as, for example, the five aggregates are not different from their nature of impermanence and their nature of suffering.
If they were one, the wisdom of the pure realm and its universal characteristics would not be established.

Through such reasoning, it is revealed that emptiness and the false are free from the characteristics of being either identical or different; therefore, it is said that they neither exist nor do not exist, and they possess neither the characteristic of identity nor the characteristic of difference.
How should the various names be understood?
Suchness (*tathatā*) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the signless (*animitta*) and the true reality (*bhūtatā*),
the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), etc.— these are the brief enumeration of the various names for emptiness.
How should the meanings of these various names be understood?
Non-transformation, non-arrival, the cessation of characteristics, and the sphere of the noble ones;
The cause of the noble dharmas and their support— These are the sequential meanings of the various names.
Because its meaning is non-differentiation, it is called *tathatā* (suchness), for it is eternally thus and never abandons that state.
Because its meaning is the absence of inversion, it is called the *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality), for it is neither of the nature of inversion nor the object of inversion.

Its meaning is the cessation of signs; therefore, it is called signless (*animitta*). This is because it is free from all signs, because it is the objective domain of non-conceptual noble wisdom (*jñāna*), and because its essence is the wisdom of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Because the true noble dharmas arise by virtue of this object, it is therefore called the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Since the noble dharmas arise based upon this sphere as their object, the meaning of "cause" (*hetu*) here is the meaning of "realm" (*dhātu*).
The dharmakāya is established as the referent; therefore, it is called the "dharmakāya.
Thus, the meaning of the various names for emptiness has been revealed.
How should the discrimination of emptiness be understood?
It is both defiled and pure; such is the conceptualization of emptiness.
In what state or position is emptiness impure?
In what state or position is emptiness pure?
It is both with stains and without stains.
If, within this state, these various stained phenomena have not yet attained liberation and remain associated [with it], that state is described as impure.
If one emerges from all defilements at this stage, it is said that this stage is pure.
However, if one has already been associated with defilements and later becomes free of them, this is not so, because one has not escaped the nature of change and transformation.
How is it that they are not impermanent?
In response to this question, it is said:
"The water element, gold, and empty space are quiescent; the purity of the dharma-realm is likewise."
Because it is adventitious, because it is free from cessation, and because it is not a transformation of intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, there are sixteen further distinctions of this emptiness: first, internal emptiness; second, external emptiness; third, internal-and-external emptiness;

fourth, great emptiness; fifth, emptiness of emptiness; sixth, emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*); seventh, emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*); eighth, emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*); ninth, absolute emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*); tenth, emptiness of that which has no before or after; eleventh, non-abandoning emptiness; twelfth, emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*); thirteenth, emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*); fourteenth, emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*); fifteenth, emptiness of non-existence; and sixteenth, emptiness of the nature of non-existence.
Thus, one should understand emptiness as briefly explained:
the eater and the eaten are empty; the body and its basis are empty;
the seer and the suchness are empty; and that which is sought and the attainment thereof are empty.
Among these, "emptiness of the eater" is taught in reliance upon the internal sense faculties;
"emptiness of the eaten" is taught in reliance upon external objects.
The body is the locus of both the eater and the eaten; because this is a profound emptiness, it is called "internal-and-external emptiness."
The "Great Emptiness" (mahāśūnyatā) is so called because it pervades the vessel-like world; thus it is named "Great," and this emptiness is called the Great Emptiness.

The internal sense-bases (ādhyātmikāyatana), the body, and the vessel-like world—these phenomena are empty. Non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is able to perceive this emptiness; because this non-conceptual wisdom is itself empty, it is called the "Emptiness of Emptiness" (śūnyatā-śūnyatā).

When one contemplates this dharma as empty by relying on the characteristics of the ultimate truth (paramārtha) according to reason, this is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-śūnyatā).
To attain this, the bodhisattva practices emptiness; this is the emptiness of this dharma.
For what purpose is this practice undertaken?
It is for the attainment of two kinds of goodness:
first, conditioned goodness; second, unconditioned goodness. This emptiness is called the "emptiness of the conditioned and the unconditioned."

Because it is for the sake of constantly benefiting others and for the sake of exclusively and eternally benefiting others, one cultivates this emptiness; therefore, it is called "ultimate emptiness" (atyanta-śūnyatā).

In order not to abandon *saṃsāra*—wherein this *saṃsāra* has no beginning or end—sentient beings do not perceive its emptiness and, becoming weary and exhausted, they abandon *saṃsāra*. This emptiness is called "emptiness of no beginning or end" (anavarāgra-śūnyatā).
To perform good without end, even as the Buddhas enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, yet because of this emptiness not abandoning the work of benefiting others—this is called "not abandoning emptiness."

It is the nature of the pure realm (*viśuddhadhātu*). "Nature" (*dhātu*) means "category" (*gotra*), so it is designated as "nature" because it is acquired spontaneously; this emptiness is called "emptiness of nature" (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).

To obtain the great marks and minor signs—that is, the major marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and minor characteristics (*anuvyañjana*) of a Great Being—one practices this emptiness to attain these two sets of marks; this is called "emptiness of marks" (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).

For the sake of purifying the Buddha-dharma, the bodhisattva practices the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and other such unique qualities of a buddha; practicing this emptiness in order to bring about purification and emergence, it is called the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*).
Thus, having established these fourteen kinds of emptiness, one should understand how their characteristics are distinguished.
Among these fourteen, what dharma is designated as "empty"?
Both the person and dharmas are absent; herein they are called "empty."
That non-existence is not itself non-existent; within this, there is a distinct emptiness.
The non-existence of both persons and phenomena—this dharma is called "emptiness.
This dharma of non-existence is itself empty, even as it exists determinately.

Regarding the fourteen bases previously mentioned, such as the "eater" and so forth, these two phenomena are termed "emptiness. In order to reveal the true characteristic of emptiness, two types of emptiness are established at the conclusion:
first, the emptiness of non-existence; second, the emptiness of the nature of non-existence.
For what purpose are the two types of emptiness established?

It is for the sake of abandoning the superimposition (*samāropa*) of persons and phenomena, and for the sake of abandoning the denial (*apavāda*) regarding the emptiness of persons and phenomena, respectively.
In this way, the discrimination of emptiness should be understood.
How should one understand the meaning of the establishment of emptiness?
If it were said to be impure, sentient beings would have no liberation;
if it were said to be stainless, there would be no application of effort.
If all phenomena were naturally pure because they are untainted by adventitious defilements even before the antidote has arisen,
then since the afflictive obstructions would be non-existent, all sentient beings should attain liberation without relying on effort.
If the antidote has already arisen, it is by its very nature impure, because the effort of cultivating the path for the sake of attaining liberation would then be fruitless.
Since it produces such a result, it is said:
"Neither stained nor unstained, neither pure nor impure."
Because the mind is fundamentally pure, and afflictions are but adventitious dust;
how could it be neither stained nor unstained?
For the mind’s original nature is intrinsically pure.
What is neither pure nor impure?
It is because afflictions are adventitious dust.
Thus has the analysis of emptiness been briefly explained.
Regarding the establishment of the various meanings of emptiness, one should know that there are two types:
first, its essential nature (*lakṣaṇa*), and second, its formal establishment (*vyavasthāna*). What is its essential nature?
This is because of having characteristics and because of being without characteristics.
As for "having characteristics," it means being free from the characteristics of existence and non-existence, and being free from the characteristics of identity and difference.
Regarding "establishment," one should understand the differentiation of the four meanings, such as the various names and so forth.
The *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*, in its chapter on Characteristics (*Lakṣaṇapariccheda*), has completed its explanation of the verses. Regarding the pervasive [obscuration],
the one-sided [obscuration], the equal [obscuration], and the obscuration of grasping and abandoning,
I shall now explain the two kinds of obscurations.

Among these, the "universal obstruction" refers to the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obstruction to omniscience (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), because for those of the bodhisattva lineage, both obstructions are fully present.
The "partial obstruction" refers to the afflictive obstruction, pertaining to those of the śrāvaka lineage and others.
The "heavy obstruction" refers to any one of the coarse afflictions, such as desire and so forth, among the aforementioned various formations (*saṃskāra*).
The "obstruction of equality" refers to birth-and-death within any one of the formations that are equal.
Regarding the obstacles to adoption and rejection: for those of the bodhisattva lineage, these serve as obstacles to non-abiding nirvāṇa.
Thus, the two types of persons who possess obstacles corresponding to reality have been explained: first, those of the bodhisattva lineage; second, those of the śrāvaka and other lineages.
Furthermore, there are nine kinds of characteristics of afflictions (*kleśa*).

The nine fetters (*saṃyojana*) are called the obstacle of delusion (*moha-āvaraṇa*). These nine types of fetters of various delusions are here explained as the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*).
To what do these afflictive obstructions (kleśāvaraṇa) act as obstacles?
They obstruct disenchantment (nirveda), relinquishment (prahāṇa), and the vision of reality (bhūtadarśana);
specifically, the fetters of craving (tṛṣṇāsaṃyojana) obstruct the mind of disenchantment.
Regarding "the mind being firmly obstructed by hindrances," this refers to the obstruction that prevents the arising of the mind of equanimity.
Because of these delusions, one is in opposition to them; thus, within the presence of such objects, one is unable to give rise to a mind of relinquishment and abandonment.
As for the remaining fetters (*saṃyojana*), they conceal and obstruct the vision of reality.
How do obstructions arise?
They are the successive stages of these afflictions,
as well as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
The basis for the view of a self, obstacles to the Three Jewels of Cessation and the Path,
gain and honor, and so forth, as well as attachment to wealth and lack of contentment—
these various remaining afflictions are the obstacles to these five points.

Regarding the obstruction of the conceit of self (*asmimāna*): it is an obstruction that arises when one wishes to extinguish and abandon the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). In relation to the wisdom of correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana-jñāna*), there are two categories: the category of difference and the category of non-difference. Because the conceit of self frequently operates within the category of non-difference, this view of a self-identity cannot be extinguished.

The fetter of ignorance acts as an obstacle to the true vision when one seeks to distance oneself from the basis of the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), because due to it, one is unable to distance oneself from the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*).

The fetter of views acts as an obstacle when one seeks to penetrate the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*); this is because the view of a self-entity and the view of extremes give rise to fear toward the truth of cessation, while wrong view gives rise to slander toward the truth of cessation.
The fetter of grasping acts as an obstacle at the time of penetrating the Truth of the Path, because one seeks purification through the analytical investigation of specific principles.
The fetter of doubt acts as an obstacle when one wishes to penetrate the Three Jewels, because one does not have faith in or accept the virtues of the Three Jewels.
The fetter of envy acts as an obstacle when one wishes to distance oneself from gain and honor, because one fails to perceive its faults.
The fetter of avarice acts as an obstacle when one wishes to practice the lightness of wealth and contentment, because it causes one to become greedily attached to material goods and the like.
Furthermore, there are ten obstacles to the wholesome dharmas; one should know that there are also ten distinct obstacles regarding the wholesome dharmas and so forth.
What are these ten points?
Not practicing in improper places, and practicing in a manner that is not according to reason.
Not generating [the thought], not reflecting, lacking the provisions,
having an unsuitable spiritual friend, being weary of mind and thus becoming disillusioned,
practicing what is unsuitable, and dwelling together with malicious enemies.
Any one of the three coarse afflictions, the non-attainment of wisdom,
the heavy afflictions of intrinsic nature, indolence and negligence,
attachment to existence and to sensory objects, and likewise a base mind— these are the obstacles.
Lacking faith, aspiration, and joy; pondering the meaning according to the literal word;
disrespecting the Dharma while valuing gain; lacking compassion for sentient beings;
hearing of calamities or hearing little; and the reduction of the provisions for samādhi.
Regarding these various obstacles, what constitutes the wholesome dharmas?
They are: the wholesome grasping of bodhi; possessing wisdom and being free from delusive obstacles;
dedicating [merit] without fear or envy; and the ten qualities such as mastery.
Among such dharmas as the wholesome and so forth, one should know which are the obstructed and which are the obstructions. Answer:
Each of these ten has three obstructions; this should be understood within the context of the ten matters.
There are three obstacles to wholesome dharmas: first, non-cultivation; second, cultivation in an improper place; and third, irrational cultivation. There are three kinds of obstacles to bodhi:
first, the non-arising of the wholesome; second, the non-arising of correct reflection; and third, the incompleteness of the accumulations.
Regarding the "appropriation of enlightenment," the arousal of the bodhicitta is what is called the appropriation of enlightenment.
This mind has three aspects: first, conduct that is inconsistent with one's nature; second, lack of association with spiritual friends; and third, mental exhaustion and weariness.
The "one who possesses wisdom" is the essential nature of the bodhisattva; it is for the sake of knowing that this dharma has three obstacles:
first, practice that is inconsistent [with the goal]; second, dwelling together with evil friends; and third, dwelling together with malicious enemies.
In this context, "evil persons" refers to ignorant ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
"Evil and hostile persons" are those who obstruct the merits of a bodhisattva and observe their faults.
"Those without delusion" are those whose minds are not distracted; yet they possess three obstacles:

First, the coarse error of inversion; second, the afflictions and so forth; third, the presence of any one of the obstacles—these cause the remaining three [perfections] to fail to mature and the wisdom of liberation (*prajñā*) to remain immature and incomplete.
"Unobstructed" means being extinguished and separated from all hindrances; this is called "unobstructed.
There are three such hindrances: first, coarse afflictions by nature; second, indolence; and third, negligence.
There are three obstacles to the dedication of bodhi that cause the mind to dedicate itself elsewhere rather than dedicating it single-mindedly toward unsurpassed bodhi:
first, attachment to the various realms of existence; second, attachment to the dharmas that serve as the provisions for existence; and third, an inferior state of mind.

There are three obstacles to fearlessness: first, not giving rise to faith and respect toward persons; second, not giving rise to aspiration and desire for the True Dharma; and third, deliberating upon the meaning of things based merely on names and words.

Those who delight in envy have three obstacles: first, they do not respect the True Dharma; second, they respect gain, profit, and honor; and third, they do not give rise to great compassion toward sentient beings.
There are three obstacles to non-sovereignty; because of these three, one does not attain sovereignty:
first, the absence of wisdom derived from hearing; for one who lacks such hearing gives rise to karmic afflictions, which constitute a calamity to the True Dharma;
second, the paucity and weakness of wisdom derived from hearing.

Third, when the matter of samādhi is not yet matured, this [obstruction] again acts as a cause for even a single portion of each of the ten types of factors, such as those conducive to virtue (*kuśala*). Based on this meaning, one should understand which among the obstructions constitute these ten causes.
The first is the cause of arising (*utpatti-hetu*); for example, the sense-base of the eye (*cakṣur-āyatana*) acts as the cause of arising for visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
The second is the cause of subsistence (*sthiti-hetu*); for example, the four kinds of nutriment act as the cause of subsistence for all sentient beings.

Third is the cause of maintenance (*dhṛtihetu*): just as that which is maintained can be sustained by it, for example, the vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*) sustaining the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*).
Fourth is the cause of manifestation (*prakāśahetu*): just as light serves as the condition for form (*rūpa*).
Fifth is the cause of transformation (*pariṇāma-hetu*), such as fire and so forth acting upon the ripening of various things.
Sixth is the cause of separation (*viyoga-hetu*), such as a sickle and so forth acting upon the act of reaping.
Seventh is the cause of conversion (*parivartana-hetu*), such as a goldsmith or silversmith converting various gold and silver into rings, bracelets, and other ornaments.
8. The reason of necessary concomitance (*avinābhāvahetu*), such as inferring fire from smoke.
9. The reason for generating conviction (*pratyāyanahetu*), such as establishing the probandum by means of the constituent parts of the proof-reason (*sādhanāṅga*).
Tenth is the cause of attainment (*prāpti-hetu*): for example, the Path and so forth act as causes for various fruits such as Nirvāṇa.
In this way, one should understand that it obstructs birth in wholesome states, because it is intended to bring [the fruit] into existence.
The obstacle to abiding refers to the locus of enlightenment, because this should not be corrupted or disturbed.
The obstacle to sustaining refers to the locus of the embrace of enlightenment, because the bodhicitta is able to sustain it.
The obstacle to clear comprehension refers to that which possesses the capacity for cognition, because it ought to be clearly manifested.
The obstacle to transformation refers to that which is free from delusion; since delusion undergoes cessation, there is transformation.
The separation from obstacles refers to the locus of non-obstruction, as its essential nature is the separation from these obstacles.
The turning away from obstacles refers to the locus of dedication, as its essential characteristic is the dedication of the bodhicitta.
That which necessarily obstructs comparison is the absence of fear; yet because of lack of faith, one fears.
That which obstructs faith is the absence of envy; for by not being envious of the Dharma, one causes others to have faith.
Regarding the obstacles to attainment: they pertain to the state of mastery, which is characterized by being unattached and having attainment as its essential nature.
Furthermore, there are other distinct obstacles concerning the ten perfections of the stages that assist the path.
Regarding the section on the factors that assist the path (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*):
The bases consist of lack of clarity and indolence, the two types of deficiency in samādhi,
non-cultivation and weakness, and the faults of various coarse and evil views.
Regarding the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), lack of clarity regarding the objective basis constitutes an obstacle.
Regarding the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), laziness is the obstacle.
Regarding the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), deficiency in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is the obstacle.
Two factors constitute incompleteness.
Regarding the four—desire, diligence, mind, and investigation—if any one is lacking, cultivation is incomplete; this is because one of the eight factors that constitute the provisions is absent.
Regarding the stage of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*), it is not inferior because it contains the seeds of the wholesome dharmas conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
Regarding the stage of the powers (*bala*), it refers to when those same five faculties are weak because they arise in association with factors that do not assist the path.
In the context of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), there are the faults of various views, because they are manifested by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
In the context of the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), there are coarse and evil faults, because they are manifested by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Regarding the obstacles to the *pāramitās*:
[the obstacle of] wealth and noble rebirths; the obstacle of not relinquishing sentient beings;
the loss through the increase or decrease of merit; and causing all sentient beings to enter [into the path].
Liberation is immeasurable; it causes goodness to be uninterrupted, its activity is always resolute, and through its common application, it brings others to maturity.
These ten perfections (*pāramitā*) can give rise to this Dharma; this Dharma is the fruit of the perfections.
Because they constitute obstacles to the fruit of the pāramitās, the obstacles to the pāramitās are thus explicitly taught.
What dharma constitutes an obstacle to the dāna-pāramitā?
It is the obstacle consisting in the lack of mastery and supremacy.
The perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) has as its obstacle that which obstructs the wholesome path;
the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā) has as its obstacle the abandonment of sentient beings;
the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā) has as its obstacle the increase of faults and the decrease of merit.
The dhyāna-pāramitā obstructs the transformation of sentient beings so that they may enter the forty stages of the correct position;
the prajñā-pāramitā obstructs the liberation of others.

The perfection of skillful means (upāyakauśalyapāramitā) prevents the perfections such as generosity (dānapāramitā) from being exhausted or diminished; because they are dedicated toward enlightenment, all the perfections are inexhaustible and undiminished.

The *praṇidhānapāramitā* (perfection of aspiration) consists of the uninterrupted arising [of practice] within all wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*) that obstruct rebirth in various states of existence; by virtue of the power of aspiration, it is able to sustain and follow after those wholesome qualities.

The perfection of birth (*upapatti-pāramitā*) obstructs the certainty of wholesome dharmas because the power of analytical reflection and cultivation is weak, and one is unable to subdue that which is not conducive to the path.

The perfection of wisdom (jñāna-pāramitā) is an obstacle to the enjoyment of the Dharma together with oneself and others, as well as to the maturation of both [self and others], because one does not penetrate the meaning according to the words as they are heard.
Within the ten stages, there are furthermore successive obstacles:
the meaning of pervasive supremacy, the meaning of the foremost flow of excellence,
the meaning of being without attachment, and the meaning of the non-differentiation of the body.
The meaning of stainless purity; the meaning of the non-differentiation of the Dharma-gates;
the meaning of neither decreasing nor increasing; the meaning of the basis for the four masteries—this ignorance regarding the dharmadhātu constitutes these ten obscurations of defilement.
It is not supported by the ten stages; rather, the various stages serve as its remedies.
Within the dharma-realm, these ten meanings pervade all places, being equal, untainted, and free from ignorance.
This ignorance should be understood as an obstruction to each of the ten bodhisattva stages in their respective order, because it is not an aid to those stages.
Within the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), what are these ten meanings?

First is the meaning of pervasiveness: based on the first stage (*bhūmi*) of the bodhisattva, the meaning of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) pervades all places; by entering meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*), the bodhisattva attains thorough penetration (*prativedha*).
Through this penetration, they attain the vision of a portion of the equality of self and others.
Second is the supreme meaning: having contemplated this Dharma based on the second bhūmi, one reflects as follows:

"If liberation arises through the equality of dependence upon others and commonality, then one should apply oneself with diligence to the transformation and purification of liberation in all its aspects."

Third is the meaning of the "superior flow": because the Dharma-realm flows forth through the three stages, one knows that the sublime Dharma heard is supreme; for the sake of attaining this Dharma, one would be able to cast oneself into a fire pit as vast as a trichiliocosm.
Fourth is the meaning of being unattached to anything; because of this fourth stage, through this contemplation of dharmas, craving for existence never arises at all.
Fifth is the meaning of non-differentiation of the body; because of the fifth stage, there is the purity and equality of ten kinds of mental joy.

The sixth is the meaning of undefiled purity; it pertains to the sixth stage because, regarding the twelve bases of the causes of birth, there is not a single dharma that can be defiled or purified, as one penetrates this reality.

The seventh is the meaning of the non-differentiation of the seven dharma-gates; because in the seventh stage there is the signless (*animitta*), the distinct characteristics of various dharmas such as the sūtras do not function and are not manifested.

The eighth is the meaning of neither decreasing nor increasing; because in the eighth stage one attains the fulfillment of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and within the categories of the impure and the pure, one does not perceive even a single dharma as either decreasing or increasing.
Within this, there are furthermore four kinds of mastery.
What are the four? First, mastery over non-conceptuality; second, mastery over the pure land; third, mastery over gnosis; and fourth, mastery over karma.
Among these, the dharma-dhātu is the basis for the first and second masteries.
On the eighth stage, there is the meaning of the basis for mastery over knowledge through thorough penetration, because one attains the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence on the ninth stage.
Regarding the meaning of mastery over karma, it refers to performing deeds for the benefit of sentient beings through transformations according to one's will based on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Furthermore, there is a brief explanation.
Having already explained the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obstructions to omniscience (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), [the following is said]:
This encompasses all obstacles; by exhausting them, one attains liberation.
Because these two kinds of obstacles are extinguished without remainder, one achieves transcendence and liberation from all obstacles.

The general meaning of the obstructions is as follows: first, the great obstruction, because it is all-pervasive; second, the minor obstruction, because it obstructs only one direction; third, the obstruction to practice, which consists of heavy afflictions (*kleśa*); fourth, the obstruction to attainment, which consists of pervasive afflictions (*paryavasthāna*); fifth, the obstruction to the excellence of attainment and the obstruction of acceptance and rejection; sixth, the obstruction to right practice, which consists of the nine kinds of fetters of affliction; seventh, the causal obstruction, because of the ten types of causal meanings regarding wholesome states and so forth; eighth, the obstruction to entering reality, which is the obstruction to the aids to the path (*bodhipakṣa*); ninth, the obstruction to unsurpassed goodness, which is the obstruction to the ten perfections (*pāramitā*); and tenth, the obstruction of acceptance, rejection, and detachment.
The obstacles subsumed within the ten stages are briefly stated to be of two kinds:
first, the obstacle to liberation; second, the obstacle to omniscience.
This concludes the second chapter, the "Chapter on Obstacles," of the *Madhyāntavibhāga*.
Chapter Three: On Reality (Tattva-varga). This chapter on reality should now be explained. What is reality?
It is the reality of fundamental characteristics and the reality free from inversion.
The reality of both fruit and cause, The reality of the subtle and the coarse,
The accomplishment of the pure realm, And the reality of the analytical division of the constituents—
These ten types of ultimate reality of supreme wisdom Serve as the antidote to the view of self.
Regarding these ten kinds of reality, what are the ten?

First, fundamental reality; second, reality of characteristics; third, reality free from inversion; fourth, reality of cause and fruit; fifth, reality of the subtle and the coarse; sixth, reality of accomplishment; seventh, reality of the pure sphere; eighth, reality of inclusion; ninth, reality of analytical division; tenth, reality of superior wisdom.
Furthermore, it should be understood that there are ten kinds of superior knowledge regarding reality (*tattva*), which serve as antidotes to the ten kinds of self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*).

What are these ten? First, superior knowledge of the aggregates (*skandha*); second, superior knowledge of the elements (*dhātu*); third, superior knowledge of the sense-bases (*āyatana*); fourth, superior knowledge of the conditions for birth; fifth, superior knowledge of what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna*); sixth, superior knowledge of the faculties (*indriya*); seventh, superior knowledge of time (*adhvan*); eighth, superior knowledge of the truths (*satya*); ninth, superior knowledge of the vehicles (*yāna*); and tenth, superior knowledge of the conditioned and the unconditioned (*saṃskṛta-asaṃskṛta*).
Among these, what is fundamental reality?
It consists of the three natures: first, the imagined nature; second, the dependent nature; and third, the perfected nature.
All other realities are established within this [system].
Among the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), which phenomena are called "realities" that can be trusted and accepted?
One nature is eternally non-existent; two exist but are not real.
The three realms of existence are not real; these three are fundamentally real.
That which is characterized by the nature of conceptual construction is eternally non-existent.
This characteristic is real within the nature of conceptual construction, because it is free from inversion.
Regarding the characteristic of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*): it is unreal because it exists only as the arising of distracted grasping.
This dependence within the dependent nature is its true nature (*tathatā*).
Regarding the characteristic of the true nature: it is the reality of existence and non-existence.
This characteristic is real within the nature of reality.
What is the characteristic that is real?
It is the denial through exaggeration or depreciation regarding phenomena and persons.
Regarding the grasped and the grasper, and all views concerning existence and non-existence,
when one knows that the view of permanence does not arise,

this is the characteristic of true quiescence. Because one knows and sees these phenomena, the views of superimposition— such as regarding persons and dharmas— and the views of deprecation cannot arise.

Within this nature of conceptual differentiation (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), this is the true characteristic; thus, views of exaggeration (*samāropa*) or depreciation (*apavāda*) regarding the grasper and the grasped cannot arise, for the purpose of knowing and seeing this dharma.

This dharma is the true characteristic within the dependent nature; because one knows and perceives this dharma, views of superimposition and denial—which would posit existence where there is no existence—cannot arise.
Within this true nature of phenomena, this is the characteristic of reality; such a fundamental characteristic of reality is called the "reality of characteristics" and the "unmistaken reality."
Non-erroneous reality refers to that which serves as the antidote to errors such as the notion of permanence;
it is fourfold: first, impermanence; second, suffering; third, emptiness; and fourth, non-self.
What are these four?
They are established based on fundamental reality.
In this context, how should impermanence be understood?
The meaning of impermanence has three aspects: the meaning of non-existence, the meaning of arising and ceasing, and the meaning of being with or without defilement;
these follow the sequence within fundamental reality (*tattva*).
Within fundamental reality there are three natures; one should understand that within these natures, the three meanings of impermanence follow their respective order.
First, it is taught as impermanent because its meaning is the absence of any substantial entity;
second, its meaning is arising and ceasing;
third, its meaning is being defiled or undefiled.

There are three types of suffering: first, the suffering of grasping (*upādāna-duḥkha*); second, the suffering of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-duḥkha*); and third, the suffering of association (*saṃprayoga-duḥkha*).

Among the faculties (*indriya*) and within the ultimate reality (*tattva*), these three kinds of suffering follow in sequence: first, the suffering of grasping, because it is that which is grasped through attachment to persons and phenomena;
second, the suffering of characteristics, because the three feelings (*vedanā*) have the three types of suffering as their characteristics.
Regarding "suffering through association":
because it is associated with the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*),
and because it is the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of conditioned phenomena, these three types of suffering should be established within the sequence of their nature.
Non-emptiness is not unlike emptiness; the nature of emptiness accords with these three types.
Regarding the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), there is no separate principle by which the non-existence of an entity constitutes its emptiness.

Regarding the characteristic of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*): it does not exist in the manner in which it is conceptualized; yet this phenomenon is not entirely non-existent, for it exists as emptiness.

Regarding the characteristic of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*): it is the intrinsic nature of the two kinds of emptiness; therefore, it is called "emptiness of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
The signless, the distinct signs, and the self-characteristics—the three kinds of selflessness.
Regarding the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), its characteristic essence does not exist; therefore, this "signless" is its selflessness.
The dependent nature has characteristics that do not exist in the manner they are conceptualized; that these characteristics do not exist as they appear is its selflessness.
The perfected nature is the absence of both [types of] self; therefore, its very essence is selflessness.
Within these three kinds of fundamental reality, three types of impermanence are explained:
first, the impermanence of non-existence; second, the impermanence of arising and ceasing; and third, the impermanence of being with or without defilement.
The three kinds of suffering:
first, the suffering of grasping; second, the suffering of characteristics; third, the suffering of association.
The three kinds of emptiness:
The three kinds of emptiness: first, the emptiness of non-existence; second, the emptiness of non-conformity with space;

third, the emptiness of intrinsic nature. The three kinds of selflessness: first, the selflessness of signlessness; second, the selflessness of distinct signs; third, the selflessness of intrinsic nature.
Regarding the reality of cause and fruit: within this fundamental reality, what should be established as cause and fruit?
They are the truth of suffering, the truth of origination, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path.
How is fundamental reality established?
The characteristics of suffering and so forth have already been explained; the truth of suffering is as previously stated.

Within the reality of non-perversion, such as the three types of suffering and the three types of impermanence, one should understand the truth of suffering through these four aspects of non-perversion.
One should know that there are three types of the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*). What are these three?
The truth of origination further consists of three: habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*), arousal (*samutthāna*), and [the resulting] manifestation.
Regarding "non-separation" and so forth:
the perfuming that constitutes the truth of accumulation (*saṃudaya-satya*) refers to the attachment to the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
The perfuming that gives rise to the truth of accumulation consists of afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma.
Regarding the truth of origination as inseparable: it is like suchness being inseparable from the afflictive obscurations.
One should understand the truth of cessation through its threefold meaning of cessation. What are these three?
The essence and cessation are two kinds of cessation: the cessation of defilement and purity, occurring sequentially.
Self-nature is non-arising; thus, the two dharmas of the grasper and the grasped do not arise.
There are two kinds of the quiescent cessation of defilement: first, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and second, the suchness of dharmas (*dharmatā*).
Regarding these three kinds of cessation—first, cessation as non-existence; second, cessation as duality;
and third, cessation as intrinsic nature—and the three aspects of the truth of the path, how are they established within the three fundamental realities?
Contemplative wisdom, elimination, and realization constitute the three aspects of the Path.

The Truth of the Path is thus explained: first, the contemplation of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature); second, the contemplation for the elimination of the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature); and third, the contemplation for the realization of the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature).
Thus, within this context, it should be understood that the Truth of the Path is established for the purposes of investigation, eradication, and realization.
As for "coarse and subtle reality," these refer to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
How can these two truths be established within fundamental reality?
There are three types of coarse meanings: the establishment of names, the grasping of formations, and that which is clearly manifest—these are called conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).

There are three kinds of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*): first, conventional truth as the establishment of names; second, conventional truth as the engagement in practice; and third, conventional truth as clear manifestation.
Based on these three meanings, one should understand that within fundamental reality (*mūla-tattva*), three types of conventional truth are to be established in their respective order.
Regarding "one among the three truths is the truth of the supreme object": one should understand that this supreme object exists within the single true nature (*tathatā*).
What is this true nature? It is:
first, the true nature of the object; second, the true nature of correct cultivation; and third, the true nature of attainment.
The reality of meaning (*arthatattva*) is so called because it is the objective domain of the true wisdom regarding the suchness of phenomena (*dharmatathatā*).
The reality of attainment (*prāptitattva*) is so called because it is the ultimate perfection of the merits of *nirvāṇa*.
The reality of correct practice (*pratipattitattva*) is so called because there is no superior state beyond the noble path (*āryamārga*).
How are conditioned and unconditioned phenomena both subsumed within the attainment of true reality? Answer:
Being immutable and non-erroneous, they accomplish the two kinds of true reality.
As for unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), they are accomplished without change and are included within the inclusion of true reality (*tathatā*).
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are subsumed under the Path because they are accomplished without inversion and because there is no inversion within the categories of their objects.
Regarding the "accomplishment of reality," how is it within fundamental reality?
As for the establishment of accomplishment: it is established in a single locus as conventional.

It is established within the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); because one repeatedly practices the signs and determinations established for that object in common with others, worldly cognition arises based on those established signs and determinations.

All people in the world possess the same worldly knowledge regarding a single object: they agree that "this thing is earth and not fire," or "this thing is visible form and not sound. In this way, such conventional accomplishments belong to a single nature.
Because that which is devoid of designation lacks intrinsic nature, the principle of establishment in three locations is fulfilled.

These are the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). For those of superior faculties who are clever regarding both meaning and principle, when they abide in the stage of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), they achieve the accomplishment of either an object or a phenomenon by relying on the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and one of the four principles (*yukti*). These two are called "establishment through principle" (*yuktisiddha*).

The reality of the purified object has two aspects: first, the reality of the object of knowledge purified of the afflictive obscurations; second, the reality of the object of knowledge purified of the cognitive obscurations. Such is the reality of the purified object of knowledge.
The two kinds of pure objects are subsumed within a single locus.
This single locus is the nature of reality (*tathatā*). Why is this so?
Because it is the object of pure wisdom that is free from distinct natures, how are the five types of subsumed reality established among the three fundamental realities?
Characteristics and conceptualization are subsumed under two natures: the nature of characteristics and the nature of names.
In accordance with the meaning, based on the fivefold categories of inclusion,
how can the characteristic and the conceptualized be established within the fundamental nature, and how are they included within the dependent nature?
"Name" is subsumed within the nature of conceptual differentiation (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Holy wisdom (*āryajñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*)—these two are subsumed within a single nature.
Suchness and holy wisdom are both subsumed within the nature of ultimate reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
How is the reality of analytical investigation established within the three types of fundamental natures?
There are seven kinds of reality of analytical investigation. What are these seven?
Birth and reality are subsumed under the two natures; the same applies to the bases and misconduct.
Characteristics, consciousness, and purification are subsumed under correct practice and true nature.

First, the reality of origination; second, the reality of characteristics; third, the reality of consciousness; fourth, the reality of the basis; fifth, the reality of wrong practice; sixth, the reality of purification; and seventh, the reality of right practice.

Regarding the *pariniṣpanna-tattva* (the reality of perfected accomplishment), it should be understood as existing within two locations among the fundamental realities: the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) and the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).

Just as with the *pariniṣpanna-tattva*, the same applies to the *paratantra-tattva* (reality of dependent origination) and the *mithyā-pratipatti-tattva* (reality of erroneous practice); these are subsumed within two natures within the fundamental reality.
The four dharmas—characteristics, consciousness, purity, and correct practice—are subsumed within a single reality-nature (*tathatā*).
How are these four types subsumed within a single nature?
Because they are manifested by the noble objects and noble wisdom.
The reality of supreme wisdom is taught as an antidote to the ten kinds of views of self.
What are the ten kinds of views of self regarding the aggregates and so forth?
First: the cause and the enjoyer, the agent and the sovereign.
The sense of superiority and permanence, the basis for defilement and purification,
the observer, and that which is bound or liberated— within these [factors], the view of self arises. Thus,
these ten kinds of false attachments to a self arise with respect to the aggregates and other phenomena.
To counteract ten kinds of false attachments, ten kinds of supreme wisdom are taught.

What are these ten kinds of false attachments regarding a self? First, attachment to unity; second, attachment to causality; third, attachment to a recipient; fourth, attachment to an agent; fifth, attachment to sovereignty; sixth, attachment to supremacy; seventh, attachment to permanence; eighth, attachment to being defiled or purified; ninth, attachment to a beholder; and tenth, attachment to one who binds or liberates.
How is it established within the fundamental reality of the ten kinds of supreme wisdom?
It is because the five aggregates and all other phenomena are subsumed within the three natures according to their respective principles.
How can one abide within the three natures?
There are the colors of conceptualization (*parikalpita*), the colors of differentiation (*vikalpa*), and the colors of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Thus, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has three kinds.
First, there is the discrimination of form, which is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) of the sense-field of form.
Second, there are the varieties of form, which are the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) of the sense-field of form.
Why is it called "dependent"?
Among these five established dharmas, because their essential natures differ, they are established under distinct categories as "form" (*rūpa*).
Three of these dharmas are thus form; the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) is its true nature, for it is the common characteristic of form.

As it is with form (*rūpa*), so it is with the other aggregates (*skandha*) such as sensation (*vedanā*); and the same applies to all phenomena (*dharma*) within the elements (*dhātu*) and sense-bases (*āyatana*).

Because they should be equally subsumed within the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), one should understand that this is likewise the case regarding the ten kinds of superior knowledge (*daśavidhajñāna*) and the two realities (*tattva*), namely the reality of ultimate truth (*paramārthatattva*) and the fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*).
It has already been stated that the superior wisdom regarding the five aggregates and so forth serves as the antidote to the ten kinds of views of self;
however, the meaning of the five aggregates and so forth has not yet been explained. This meaning is now explained:
"Neither unity nor a mere collection, but differentiation—this is the meaning of 'aggregate' (*skandha*)."

There are three meanings for the establishment of the term "aggregate" (skandha). First, regarding the establishment of the meaning: the name "aggregate" has three senses: first, the sense of a path; second, the sense of burning heat; and third, the sense of a heavy burden.
Furthermore, the meaning of "accumulation" (skandha) is the meaning of "aggregate.
There are three meanings of "accumulation": first, the sense of "multiplicity," as stated in the sūtras:
"Whether form is past, present, or future; whether distant or near; whether coarse or subtle," and so forth, as explained at length in the sūtras.
Because this form is manifold, it is called an "aggregate" (*rāśi*).
In this way, such forms are subsumed within a single location.

This statement indicates a collective enumeration of the aggregates (*skandha*) such as form; because their essential natures and characteristics are diverse and because they do not mutually encompass one another, they are said to have distinctions.
These three meanings—multiplicity, totality, and distinction—are called the meaning of "aggregation" (skandha).
Aggregation is precisely the meaning of "aggregate" (rāśi); by virtue of this meaning, it resembles the worldly notion of a heap.
The grasper, the grasped, and the act of grasping—these seeds are the meaning of "element" (*dhātu*).
Furthermore, there is another inclusive sense of "element.
What meaning does the term "element" signify?
This clarifies the meaning of seeds.
The seeds that function as the grasper are called the various elements (dhātus) such as the eye;
the seeds that function as the grasped are the various elements such as form.
That which takes up the seeds refers to the various elements such as consciousness.
Because they function to receive and differentiate sensory objects, and because they serve as gateways, they are called "entrances" (*āyatana*).

Furthermore, there are distinct dharmas named entrances; herein, the three types of sensation constitute the "reception," and because they are the gateways for these three sensations, the six internal entrances are taught.
Because they distinguish between objective realms and the gateways of experience, the six external bases are taught.
What is the meaning of the twelve links of dependent origination?
Their meaning consists in cause, effect, and activity, without addition or subtraction.
The meaning of cause, effect, and activity—neither adding to nor subtracting from their true nature—is what is called the meaning of the twelve links of dependent origination.
To "add to" the cause refers to establishing unequal causes through various conceptual constructions, such as those regarding formative factors (*saṃskāra*) and so forth.
The diminution of causes refers to the conceptual establishment of the meaning of causelessness.

The augmentation of effects refers to the conceptualization that the various formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth arise in dependence upon ignorance while possessing a self (*ātman*). Such is the conceptualization.
Regarding the diminution of the fruit: it is the [erroneous view] that phenomena such as volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) do not arise from ignorance (*avidyā*).

Regarding the exaggeration of the entity: it is the [erroneous view] that causes such as ignorance produce fruits such as volitional formations, and that there is a deliberate agent involved in the temporal differentiation [of these processes].
Regarding the matter of diminution: because one discriminates [the absence of] effortlessness (*anābhoga*).

When one is free from these two attachments regarding the matters of cause and effect, this principle is without superimposition and without diminution; thus should the meaning of the twelve links of dependent origination be understood.
Non-desire, desire for purity, co-nascence, predominance, acquisition,
and the undertaking of practice— these have the sense of being dependent on another.
There are seven kinds of the possible and the impossible, because they have the sense of being dependent on another.
It should be understood that herein, first, regarding those who do not wish to be bound to others: due to unwholesome conduct, they may not wish to enter the evil realms definitively.
Second, regarding those who wish to be bound to others: due to wholesome conduct, they enter the good realms, yet they may not wish to enter them definitively.

Regarding the three types of dependence on others for purification: if one does not abandon the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), does not cultivate the seven factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), and does not reach the end of suffering, [one remains dependent].

Regarding the four types of co-arising dependence on others: two Tathāgatas do not appear before or after one another, and two wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*) cannot co-arise within a single world-system.
Fifth, regarding the bondage of being subject to another: a woman cannot become a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*).
Sixth, regarding the bondage of having attained dependence on another: a woman cannot become a *pratyekabuddha* or a Buddha.

Seventh, regarding those whose undertaking of actions is dependent upon others: one who has already seen the Four Truths cannot perform actions such as killing, because it is only ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who are capable of performing such actions.
This is explained in detail in the *Bahudhātuka-sūtra*; one should investigate accordingly.
Regarding the faculties (*indriya*), there are twenty-two kinds. Based on six meanings, the Buddha established the twenty-two faculties.
Furthermore, there are another six meanings. What are these six?
Appropriation, maintenance, and connection; enjoyment, and the two kinds of purity.

Because they function as the predominant factors (*adhipati*) among these six matters—ranging from the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*) as their object to the two kinds of purity as their object—the twenty-two dharmas are designated as "faculties" (*indriya*).
Because they exercise predominance over the apprehension of the six objects, the six factors beginning with the eye are called faculties (*indriya*).
Because they exercise predominance in maintaining the continuity [of existence] until the end of birth and death, life-force (*jīvitendriya*) is said to be a faculty.
The male and female faculties are taught as predominant for the continuity of worldly existence.
The five sensations are taught as faculties because they are predominant in experience.
The five factors beginning with faith are taught as faculties because the activities of the mind and so forth are experienced through them, and because they are predominant in mundane purification.
For the sake of the transcendental purity that is predominant, the three untainted faculties—namely, "the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown,'" etc.—are taught as roots.
The fruit and its cause have already been experienced; there is that which has been utilized and that which has not yet been utilized.
Furthermore, there is another [classification], namely the "three times" (*trikāla*), which corresponds to their respective meanings.
Because the cause and effect have already been utilized, the past time (*atīta-adhvā*) is established.
Because the cause and effect have not yet been utilized, the future time (*anāgata-adhvā*) is established.
Because the cause has already been exhausted while the fruit is not yet exhausted, the present world is established.
Sensation and the requisites for sensation act as the causes for the arising of those formations;
their cessation and their antidote constitute, respectively, the impure and the pure.
Furthermore, there is another classification called the Four Truths. What are these four?
The first is the Truth of Suffering.
What phenomena are called suffering?
They are sensation and the requisites for sensation,
as it is said in the Sūtra:
All sensations are suffering. One should understand that the requisites for sensation,
the conditions for the arising of sensation, and all phenomena such as the faculties and their objects serve as the causes for producing those formations (*saṃskāra*).
What is the truth of origination?
It consists of all unwholesome conduct that brings about various forms of suffering.
Its cessation and its antidote constitute this [truth of] impurity and purity.
Because these two dharmas—cause and effect—are quiescent, they are called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
To counteract these two, there is the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
Based on this conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one speaks of impurity; based on this ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one speaks of purity.
Without discrimination between gain and loss, wisdom leads to liberation through others;
by means of wisdom, one attains liberation for oneself.
Furthermore, there is another classification called the Three Vehicles, which should be understood as corresponding to their respective meanings.

Because the wisdom that contemplates nirvana and saṃsāra, as well as virtues and faults, arises from hearing from others and attaining liberation based on others regarding cause and effect, it is designated as the Śrāvaka-yāna.
Therefore, as previously explained, when wisdom does not arise from others nor depend on the practice of others for the sake of liberation from cause and effect, it is called the Pratyekabuddhayāna.
One should know that when one relies on non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) to achieve liberation from cause and effect by oneself, this is called the Mahāyāna.

There are those that have verbal expression and causes, those with characteristics and conditioned phenomena, as well as the meaning and object of tranquility; these are followed by the explanation of unconditioned phenomena.
There are distinct names for the conditioned and the unconditioned.
"Discourse" refers to names, phrases, and phonemes.
"Cause" refers to the ālayavijñāna as comprised of seeds.

"Characteristics" refer to the receptacle world, the body, and that which is enjoyed, as well as the mind and the grasping of conceptualization as comprised by the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
Such phenomena as these possess verbal expression, causes, characteristics, and associated factors; these are called conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Among these, that which is called "mind" (*citta*) is the phenomenon that constantly arises with the characteristic of cognizing and the characteristic of discerning.
"Apprehension" refers to the five consciousnesses and the discriminating mental consciousness, because these possess three kinds of discrimination.
"Unconditioned phenomena" (asaṃskṛta-dharma) refers to the meaning of tranquility and the object of tranquility.
The meaning of tranquility is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
The object of tranquility is the suchness (*tathatā*) of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
In this context, why is the Truth of the Path designated by the name "tranquility"?
If this dharma takes an object as its condition, or manifests the fruit based on tranquility, then by virtue of this meaning,
the five aggregates and so forth— the ten bases, noble wisdom, and the skillful means of noble wisdom— should be known as the ten types of supreme knowledge.
These ten are called the "realities.
Regarding the meaning of their combination as realities, if explained briefly, there are two kinds of reality:
first, that which manifests reality, such as a mirror;
The reality manifested by these two is like a reflection.
What is it that manifests this reality?
It is the three fundamental realities, because through them the remaining realities are made manifest.
There are nine kinds of reality as it is manifested: first, the reality manifested by the absence of overweening pride;
second, the reality manifested by the remedy for perversions;
third, the reality manifested by the renunciation of the Śrāvaka vehicle; [and so forth].
The reality manifested by the renunciation of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle;
and fifth, the reality manifested by the renunciation of the Mahāyāna.
By means of this coarse reality, sentient beings and phenomena are established; as for the subtle reality, it brings liberation to sentient beings and phenomena.
Sixth, the reality revealed by those who cause opponents to fall into positions of defeat through the use of correct analogies and correct reasoning;
