seventh, the reality revealed by the elucidation of the Mahāyāna;
eighth, the reality revealed by the inclusion of all phenomena within all aspects of the knowable.
Ninth, the reality revealed as the non-conformity and conformity with what is revealed;
tenth, the reality revealed by the entry into the meaning of all phenomena that serve as the basis for the grasping of a self.
This concludes the "Chapter on Reality" from the *Madhyāntavibhāga-mahāyāna-śāstra*.

Chapter Four: Cultivation of the Counteractive Practices. Regarding the cultivation of the counteractive practices, the cultivation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment shall now be explained.
In this treatise, "mind" is first explained as a category of self-clinging; it is also described as the sense faculties, objects, and consciousness.

Because they are the causes of coarse conduct and craving, because they are the seeds [of existence], and because they are not deluded, one practices the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness in order to enter the Four Noble Truths.
Through the body, coarse formations (*audārikasaṃskāra*) become manifest; by discerning these coarse formations, one enters into the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
This body is gross and vast because its characteristic is that of various formations.

That which is coarse and gross is called the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). Because of this suffering of conditioned existence, the Noble Ones contemplate all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) therein as the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
Feeling (*vedanā*) is the basis for craving; by discerning these feelings, one enters into the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).

The mind (*citta*) is the locus of the grasping at a self; by investigating this mind, one enters the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*), thereby becoming free from the fear of annihilation regarding the self.

Phenomena (*dharma*) consist of the two categories of the impure and the pure; by investigating these phenomena, one becomes free from ignorance concerning the impure and pure categories and thus enters the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
Therefore, the initial practice is established for the purpose of entering into the Four Noble Truths by cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness;
next, one cultivates the right efforts.
Having understood what does not assist the path, [one applies] the remedies of every kind.
For the sake of the two aforementioned types, one cultivates the four right efforts.

This is for the sake of bringing the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness to completion, because all aspects of both the unwholesome factors that hinder the path and the wholesome factors that assist the path have been clearly understood through direct vision.
In order to abandon factors that do not assist the path and to give rise to factors that do assist the path, the four kinds of right exertion (*samyakpradhāna*) arise.

The first is for the purpose of abandoning unwholesome and evil states that have already arisen; as explained at length in the Sūtras, this is for the sake of their cessation, obstruction, non-arising, and non-increase.
Abiding therein according to the task at hand, for the sake of accomplishing what is required,
and in order to abandon the five faults, one cultivates the eight provisions.

Having cultivated right effort for the sake of abandoning and attaining the two types of phenomena— the black and the white— the mind, being free from hindrances and possessing assistance, comes to abide in this state.
The bases of power (ṛddhipāda) possess four capabilities.
As for these four capabilities: first, the attainment of accomplishment in accordance with instruction.
"Attainment of accomplishment in accordance with instruction" refers to what is called the four bases of power, because they are the causal conditions for accomplishing all sought-after aims.
In this context, "abiding" should be understood as the mind abiding, which is called *samādhi*.
Therefore, immediately after the four right efforts (*samyak-pradhāna*), the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are taught in succession.

It should be understood that abiding according to the object and according to the instruction is for the sake of eliminating five kinds of faults and for the sake of cultivating eight kinds of provisions.
What are called the "losses"? Laziness,
forgetting the venerable instructions, as well as inferiority, agitation, non-attention,
and [inappropriate] attention— these five losses should be known.
The indolent person sinks into the state of sloth and evil.
One who forgets the venerable teaching fails to recollect or uphold the dharmas established by the Teacher, such as the system of words, phrases, and syllables.
Regarding the inferiority of agitation (*auddhatya*), the two obstacles are combined into one because they take joy and sorrow as their essence; thus, sinking and floating are its manifestations.
Within this state, failing to apply attention when one is sinking constitutes the fourth fault.
If one applies mental attention without these two, this is the fifth fault.
To eliminate these five faults, eight kinds of requisites for meditative concentration are established in order to eliminate laziness.
What are these four? First, desire; second, right effort; third, faith; and fourth, serenity.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas that should be understood in their proper sequence.
The basis and that which depends upon it: these are the cause-and-condition and the fruit.
"Desire" is the basis for right effort; "that which depends upon it" is right effort itself. This basis is called desire.
What is the cause by which this is called faith?

If there is faith, then desire arises; this "reliant factor" (āśraya) is called the fruit of right effort (samyak-vyāyāma), and this fruit is called tranquility (praśrabdhi), because through the application of right effort, one attains the meditative concentration (dhyāna) sought.
The remaining four kinds of provisions are: first, mindfulness; second, wisdom; third, mental attention; and fourth, equanimity and cessation.
The remaining four kinds of faults are countered by these [provisions] in their respective order.
These four dharmas, beginning with mindfulness, should be understood in their proper sequence:
not being deluded regarding the object of focus, being able to discern its high and low [qualities],
extinguishing the mental effort directed toward it, and relinquishing it during the state of tranquility.
Mindfulness (*smṛti*) is not forgetting the object.
Wisdom (*prajñā*) is, at the time of not forgetting the object, being aware of the two states of sinking and floating.
Having become aware of them, one applies effort to eliminate these; this is called attention (*manasikāra*).
Once these two dharmas of sinking and floating have been stilled, the arising of a mind of equanimity that flows forth in continuity is called "equanimous cessation.
Following the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the cultivation of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) is explained in succession.
How are these five faculties established?
Because they have already attained the seeds of liberation, because desire is predominant,
because they are not deluded or submerged by objects, and because they are neither distracted nor [merely] analytical.
In this context, the flow through these five stages of increasing supremacy is for the sake of cultivating the four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*).

Because the mind has already become established in accordance with the teaching, it thereby plants the seeds of the roots of virtue conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*): first, due to the supremacy of aspiration; second, due to the supremacy of diligent cultivation; third, due to the supremacy of non-forgetfulness regarding the object; fourth, due to the supremacy of non-distraction; and fifth, due to the supremacy of discerning phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*).
The five faculties, beginning with faith, should be understood according to their sequence.
It is said that the powers (bala) destroy the afflictions; thus, the former are the cause and the latter are the fruit.
The five dharmas, beginning with faith, are as previously described.
They are called "powers" (*bala*) because they possess superior strength.
What is the meaning of "superior strength"?
It is the capacity to impair, abandon, and not assist the afflictions.

If the five dharmas—faith and the others—are not the antidotes to the various afflictions, because they do not mutually obstruct one another, why then is it said that the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*) have a sequential order?
How is it that these five dharmas, faith and the rest, are taught in their specific sequence?
The five kinds of dharmas function as cause and effect in their respective order. Why is this so?
If a person has faith in the cause and faith in the result, they will resolutely apply themselves with diligence in order to attain that result.

Therefore, having practiced diligently and guarded the object of focus so that it does not shift, if mindfulness abides and the mind attains samādhi, it dwells in equanimity—neither elated nor depressed—due to two reasons: first, because of the single feeling; second, because of the single object.
Furthermore, there are five other modes of abiding that have not yet been explained:
when the mind attains concentration, one contemplates and knows the objects as they truly are.
For this reason, these five dharmas are established in their sequential order.
If a person has already planted the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*), it is said that they are at the stage of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).

If a person has already planted the roots of merit conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*), are they to be considered as being within the stage of the five faculties, or should they be considered as being within the stage of the [five] powers (*bala*)?
The two pairs of the stages leading to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) consist of the five faculties (*indriya*) and the five powers (*bala*).

The five faculties are established during the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and Summits (*mūrdhan*), while the five powers are established during the stages of Patience (*kṣānti*) and the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
If a person plants the seeds of the roots of goodness for liberation, these two stages are definitively the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
Whether they have [planted them] or not, such power is subsequently explained as the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
How is this established?
There is the section on the bases, the section on the essential nature, the third section on renunciation,
the fourth section on qualities, and the three sections on the cessation of afflictions.
The factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) are established as being manifest within the stage of the path of vision (darśanamārga). What is the meaning of "enlightenment" (bodhi)?
Non-conceptual gnosis of suchness (tathatā) is called enlightenment.
What is the meaning of "division" (*bhāga*)? To have a companion through shared activity (*samānārthatā*) is the meaning of division.

Among these seven factors, the division of the basis for awakening is called the awakening factor of mindfulness; the division of intrinsic nature is called the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmavicaya*); the division of renunciation is called the awakening factor of right effort (*vīrya*); the division of excellence is called the awakening factor of joy (*prīti*); and the three factors consisting of tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) constitute the division of non-affliction and non-obstruction.
Why are the three dharmas said to constitute the portion that is undefiled and unobstructed?
Because they serve as the causal basis and locus, and because they are expressed in terms of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Regarding the cause for being unobstructed and undefiled: it is the counteragent to the obstacle of lethargy and agitation (*styāna-middha*), which acts as the cause for heavy conduct (*dauṣṭhulya*); this is because this [state of] pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) counteracts the cause of heavy conduct.
The basis is meditative concentration;
the intrinsic nature is not abandoning the factors of enlightenment.
Next, the path-factors are explained.
How is this Dharma established?
Through the three types— distinguishing, leading to attainment, and inspiring faith in others—
and by means of the antidotes to non-conducive factors, the Eightfold Path is taught.
Within the stage of cultivating the path (*bhāvanā-mārga*), the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are established as being manifest.

The factor of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the factor of decision (*niścaya-mārga*) constitute right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). This view consists of mundane right view and the subsequently attained supramundane right view; by means of this wisdom, one definitively discerns the path and its fruit as they have been personally realized.
That which leads others to the stage of attainment consists of right thought and right speech; because there is the initiation of speech, one is able to make others understand and obtain [the truth].
That which leads others to faith consists of three types: right speech, right action, and right livelihood; these three factors follow this sequence.
Seeing [the precepts] and being content with them—this should be known as that which causes others to have faith.

Regarding the factor of causing others to have faith: when one relies on correct speech and discourse in three respects—when debating the meaning of the Dharma together and when collectively investigating its meaning—others gain confidence that this person possesses wisdom; therefore, it is called "causing others to have faith in one's wisdom."
By relying on right action (*samyak-karmānta*), others gain confidence in his observance of the precepts, because he does not perform unrighteous deeds.

By relying on right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*), others gain confidence in his light regard for wealth and his contentment; seeing that he practices according to the Dharma and in moderation regarding the four requisites of life such as clothing, they thus gain confidence in his contentment and light regard for wealth.
The section on the remedies for afflictions consists of three types: right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
These three dharmas correspond respectively to the remedies for the great afflictions, the minor afflictions, and the obstacles to mastery.
There are three types of afflictions that do not assist the path:
first, the afflictions abandoned through the cultivation of the path, which are termed "great delusions";
second, the afflictions of mental sinking and restlessness, which are termed "minor delusions."
Regarding the three obstacles to mastery, they are able to obstruct the manifestation of superior qualities.
The first obstacle is affliction (*kleśa*), for which right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*) is the antidote. Why is this so?
Because the path is accomplished through right effort, once the path is accomplished, afflictions are extinguished through reflection.
Regarding the second type of affliction, right mindfulness is its antidote.
Regarding the state of tranquil abiding, if one dwells in right mindfulness and right tranquil abiding, it is because subsidence and agitation are extinguished.
As for the third affliction, right concentration is its antidote.
Because one relies upon meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one is able to manifest the qualities of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
Regarding this cultivation of the antidotes (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*), it should be understood that, in brief, there are three kinds.
Following non-perversion there is perversion; following perversion there is non-perversion;
being without perversion and without following perversion—these are the three kinds of cultivation of the antidote.
There are three ways of cultivating the antidote.
What are the three?

First, the non-perverted dharma that is associated with perversion according to its circumstances; second, the absence of the perversion of view which is pursued by perversion; and third, the absence of perversion accompanied by the non-perverted dharma.
According to the sequence, there are distinctions in the bodhisattva’s cultivation of remedies within the stage of ordinary beings,
the stage of noble learners, and the stage of noble non-learners.
What is the distinction?
It lies in the object, the contemplation, and the attainment.
For Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, the objects of their focus are the various dharmas of the foundations of mindfulness, such as their own mental continuum and body.
If a bodhisattva takes as their objective domain all phenomena within the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) regarding the bodies and so forth of their own and others' continuums:
whereas śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas contemplate the body and other phenomena through various marks such as impermanence and so forth;
bodhisattvas, by virtue of attaining the principle of non-arising (anutpāda), contemplate and investigate them accordingly.

If śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas practice the various dharmas such as the four foundations of mindfulness, they do so for the sake of extinguishing and detaching from the body and other such phenomena;

if bodhisattvas practice these same dharmas, they do not practice them for the sake of extinguishing and detaching, nor do they practice them without the aim of extinguishing and detaching, but rather solely for the sake of attaining non-abiding nirvāṇa.
The cultivation of the remedies has already been explained.
What is the cultivation of abiding?
There are four kinds of cultivation of abiding: that of cause, entry, practice, and attainment.
There is that which is with and without mental attention; there is the superior and the unsurpassed.

The stage of aspiration and delight, the stage of entry, the stage of emergence, the stage of receiving prediction, the stage of the teacher, the stage of consecration, the stage of arrival, and the stage of merit.
The stage of performing activities has already been explained.
There are eighteen stages of cultivation and abiding.
What are these eighteen?
1. Cultivation and abiding in the causal stage (*hetu-avasthā*), when a person already abides within their own nature (*svabhāva*).
2. Cultivation and abiding in the stage of entry (*praveśa-avasthā*), having already generated the resolve for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).
3. Cultivation and abiding in the stage of practice (*caryā-avasthā*), from after generating the resolve until one has not yet reached the fruit (*phala*).
1. Abiding in cultivation at the four stages of fruition (*phala-avasthā*), which is the time when they have already been attained;
2. Abiding in cultivation at the stage with effort (*sābhoga-avasthā*), referring to noble ones still in training (*śaikṣa*);
3. Abiding in cultivation at the stage without effort (*anābhoga-avasthā*), referring to noble ones beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
The seventh stage of cultivation and abiding is that of those who have attained the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) while seeking the practice of the seven superior qualities.
The eighth stage of cultivation and abiding is that of Bodhisattvas who have transcended the stages of the Śrāvakas and others, yet have not yet entered the first ground (*prathamā bhūmi*).
Ninth is the cultivation and abiding in the stage of no higher state, which pertains to all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, as there is no further distinct stage beyond this.
Tenth is the cultivation and abiding in the stage of aspiring joy, which pertains to all bodhisattvas within the stages of practicing through aspiration and joy.
11. The cultivation and dwelling in the stage of entering is the first bodhisattva ground.
12. The cultivation and dwelling in the stage of departure consists of the six grounds following the first.
13. The cultivation and dwelling in the stage of receiving the prediction of enlightenment is the eighth ground.
Fourteenth is the stage of cultivation and abiding as a teacher capable of exposition, which is the ninth ground (*bhūmi*).
Fifteenth is the stage of cultivation and abiding of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), which is the tenth ground.
Sixteenth is the stage of cultivation and abiding of attainment, which is the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas.
The seventeenth stage of cultivation and abiding is the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) of all Buddhas.
The eighteenth stage of cultivation and abiding is the *sambhogakāya* (enjoyment body) of all Buddhas.
One should know that all such stages of abiding are immeasurable; here, they have been explained only briefly.
Furthermore, the dharma-realm has three aspects: the impure, the impure-pure, and the pure, in their respective order.
Briefly stated, there are three stages in this [realm]:
First, those abiding in the impure stage are those from the causal stage up to the stage of practice.
Second, those abiding in the impure-pure stage are the noble ones who are still in training (*śaikṣa*).
Third, those abiding in the pure stage are the noble ones who have completed their training (*aśaikṣa*).
Regarding the establishment of persons herein, one should understand it according to the principle.

Because they abide in distinct states, one should understand according to the principle that the distinctions between ordinary beings and noble ones are established: this person abides in their own nature, while this person has already entered the stage.
Thus, the cultivation and abiding have been explained.
What are the fruits obtained?
They are the fruit of the vessel, the fruit of retribution, and this is the sovereign fruit (adhipati-phala).
Delight, increase, and purity are the sequence of fruits.
Regarding the "vessel fruit," it is the maturation that corresponds with the roots of goodness.
Regarding the "retribution fruit," because the vessel fruit serves as its dominant condition, the roots of goodness reach their most supreme state.
Regarding the fruit of delight: because of repeated practice in past lives, one delights in wholesome dharmas.
Regarding the fruit of increase: because of repeatedly cultivating meritorious roots in the present life, those roots of goodness become perfected.
Regarding the fruit of purification, it consists of the cessation and departure from all obstacles.

One should understand that there are five successive types of fruits in this stage: first, the retributive fruit (*vipākaphala*); second, the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*); third, the concordant fruit (*niṣyandaphala*); fourth, the fruit of effort (*puruṣakāraphala*); and fifth, the fruit of separation (*visamyogaphala*).
The highest of the high and the first fruit, the fruit of ultimate cultivation through repeated practice,
conformity, counteraction, separation, and the superior stage—
because there is that which has a superior and that which is unsurpassed, the fruits are thus briefly explained.
Briefly stated, there are ten kinds of fruits:

first, the progressively superior fruit (*uttarottara-phala*), which should be understood as the successive stages from the generation of the mind of self-nature (*svabhāva-cittotpāda*) up to its cultivation.
Regarding the two types of the first fruit: the "initial attainment" refers to the first emergence of supramundane dharmas;
the "fruit of repeated practice" refers to the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) following the initial fruit;
and the "ultimate fruit" refers to the dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Regarding the concordant fruit, it should be understood as being due to causes and conditions.
As for the progressively superior fruit and the fruit of the antidote, these are the causes for cessation and the path; by means of these, one attains the first fruit.

Among these, the first path is called the fruit of counteraction, the fruit of separation, the fruit of repeated cultivation, and the fruit of fulfillment, for the purpose of distancing oneself from the obstacles of afflictions.
These correspond, in their respective order, to the fruits of the noble ones who are still in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The fruit of superior status consists of various merits such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
The fruit that has something superior to it refers to the bodhisattva stages (*bodhisattvabhūmi*), because they are superior to other vehicles.
The unsurpassed fruit refers to the stages of all Tathāgatas.
These four kinds of fruits are for the purpose of distinguishing the fruit of fulfillment.
To speak of them briefly, they are many; if explained extensively, they are immeasurable.

Within this context, the cultivation of the collection of various meanings of the remedies consists of: cultivation of awakening, cultivation of attenuation, cultivation of ripening, cultivation of superior matters, and secret cultivation. Because wisdom reaches the object as a single unity, there is superior cultivation, excellent cultivation, initial cultivation, middle-path cultivation, final cultivation, and cultivation with something above it.

Regarding the "unsurpassed cultivation": because there is no superior object of experience, no accumulation of deliberation, and no superior attainment, one dwells in cultivation. By synthesizing these various meanings, one should achieve dwelling in cultivation; as for "dwelling," this person dwells within their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Regarding "dwelling in the cultivation of activities": from the initial generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*) up to the stage of practice, it is called the dwelling of supreme purity, the dwelling of the stage of supreme purity, and the dwelling of the stage with adornment; because it pervades the ten stages (*bhūmi*), it is the dwelling of the unsurpassed stage.

The fruits comprise the collective meaning [of the path], namely: first, the fruit of maintenance; second, the supreme fruit; third, the fruit of prior habituation; fourth, the fruit of progressive extraction; fifth, the concise fruit; and sixth, the extensive fruit.
Among these, the "fruition of maintenance" consists of five kinds of fruits; the remaining fruits are specific variations of these five.
It is called the "fruit of maturation" because it is that which was accumulated in previous lives, and because it is drawn forth through a progressive succession of superior states.
There are four other types of results; briefly stated, there are four superior-superior results, while extensively stated, there are six concordant results.
Because these four types of results are explained in detail through their classification, this section in the *Madhyāntavibhāga* consists of three sets of four.
There are three sections: first, the section on the remedies; second, the section on the cultivation of the dwelling; and third, the section on the attainment of the fruits.

The ultimate fruit has already been explained in detail as being fivefold: first, the fruit of the vessel; second, the fruit of retribution; third, the fruit of delight; fourth, the fruit of increase; and fifth, the fruit of purification. These encompass all fruits without exception.
Chapter Seven: The Vehicle of No-Superiority. Now the Vehicle of No-Superiority shall be explained.
The Vehicle of No-Superiority has three bases: practice, the objective sphere, and the arising of the accumulation.
There are three kinds of unsurpassedness; within the Mahāyāna, it is by virtue of these three meanings that the vehicle (yāna) becomes unsurpassed.
What are the three meanings?
First, the unsurpassedness of practice; second, the unsurpassedness of the objective realm; and third, the unsurpassedness of the attainment through accumulation.
Among these, what is called "unsurpassed practice"?
It should be understood as occurring within the practice of the ten pāramitās.
Furthermore, there are six kinds of practice.
Among these ten perfections, each possesses six aspects.
What are the six? They are:
incomparability, analytical investigation, conformity with the Dharma, and freedom from extremes.
There are six types of cultivation, both specific and general.

These six cultivations are: first, incomparable cultivation; second, analytical cultivation; third, cultivation in accordance with the Dharma; fourth, cultivation free from extremes; fifth, specific cultivation; and sixth, general cultivation.
Among these, there are twelve kinds of incomparability. What are the twelve?
Vastness, long duration, supremacy, and inexhaustible essence.
Uninterrupted and unimpeded, sovereign and governing, supreme activity,
attainment, and continuity; ultimate and incomparable knowledge—
knowing these ten perfections is the incomparable meaning of this stage.
These are the twelve kinds of incomparable practices:

first, incomparable in vastness; second, incomparable in duration; third, superior; fourth, inexhaustible; fifth, uninterrupted; sixth, free from difficulty; seventh, sovereign; eighth, corrective; ninth, ultimate performance; tenth, attainment; eleventh, supreme flow; and twelfth, final consummation.
What is meant by "vast and incomparable"?
It is because one does not desire the worldly or supramundane riches and pleasures of all realms; therefore, it should be known as vast and incomparable.
What is the incomparable nature of its long duration?
It is because it is accomplished through cultivation for three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* at each stage.
What is the incomparable nature of its superiority?
Because it brings benefit to all sentient beings everywhere.
What is inexhaustible and incomparable?
It is because it is dedicated toward unsurpassed enlightenment and is thus ultimately infinite and inexhaustible.
What is the peerless uninterrupted cultivation?

It is so called because one cultivates the attainment of equal happiness for oneself and others, and because, through the merit of giving and other virtues performed for the sake of all sentient beings, one is able to fully accomplish the ten pāramitās.
What is the peerless quality of being free from difficulty?
It is because one attains the fulfillment of one's own perfections by rejoicing in the various perfections practiced by others.
What is the peerless quality of mastery?
Through the power of meditative concentrations such as the "shattering of space," the perfections of giving and the others attain fulfillment and accomplishment.
What is their incomparable cultivation?
It is because all the perfections are cultivated, refined, and protected by non-conceptual wisdom.
What is the incomparable excellence of practice?

It is because it is accomplished through the supreme *dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding dharmas) and the various factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) within the stage of practice through aspiration (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), which precedes the stages of the grounds (*bhūmi*).
What is the incomparable excellence of attainment?
Because one attains the supramundane dharmas never before seen within the first stage (*bhūmi*).
As for what constitutes the incomparable superior flow:
it should be understood that this is distinct from the first stage and pertains to the remaining eight higher stages.
What is the ultimate incomparability?
It should be understood as existing within the tenth stage and the Buddha-stage. Why is this so?

Because the bodhisattva path and the fruit of buddhahood are brought to perfection, one should understand that the ten *pāramitās* possess this meaning of incomparability. Thus, these twelve meanings of incomparability are fully contained within the ten dharmas; for this reason, the ten dharmas are collectively designated as *pāramitās*.
What are called the ten pāramitās?
To clarify the specific names of these ten dharmas, a verse is spoken:
Giving, morality, patience, diligence, concentration, wisdom, skillful means, [power, aspiration, and knowledge].
Vow, power, and gnosis—these ten are peerless perfections (*pāramitā*).
What are the specific characteristics of these ten perfections?
Not harming for the sake of material gain, and accepting [hardships] with composure to increase merit;
Eliminating evil and causing entry, liberation and inexhaustibility,
constant arising and certainty, delighting in the Dharma and the maturation of beings—
thus should one know the sequential matters of the ten pāramitās.
Through giving, a bodhisattva is able to benefit sentient beings.
Through ethical discipline, they do not harm the lives, wealth, or retinues of sentient beings.
Through patience, they remain mentally composed and endure when others inflict harm or distress upon them.
Through diligence, one causes the growth of others' virtues and the diminution of their karmic obstacles and hindrances.

Through meditative concentration, by means of various qualities such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), one causes other sentient beings to turn away from evil and return to the good, enabling them to enter the stage of correctness (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Through *prajñā*, one elucidates the true teaching to bring others to liberation;
through *upāya*, one dedicates the roots of virtue toward great enlightenment, ensuring that the merits of generosity and other virtues flow forth inexhaustibly.

By the power of their vows, they are able to take birth in whatever realm they desire and dwell there with equanimity; within those births, they are able to serve all Buddhas and hear the true Dharma, and they constantly and unceasingly practice generosity and the other perfections to benefit sentient beings. By the power of analytical reflection and cultivation, they subdue and eliminate opposing factors, and are thus decisively able to practice the various perfections such as generosity to benefit sentient beings.

Through wisdom, they eliminate the ignorance regarding phenomena as they are expressed in words; thus, practices such as giving and the phenomena that serve as the predominant conditions for such practices become available for common enjoyment.
These two types of bodhisattvas are able to bring sentient beings to maturity.
The practice of the peerless has already been explained.
What is the practice of reflection? It is as follows:
while proclaiming the True Dharma, one reflects upon the meaning of the Mahāyāna.
This is the constant practice of the Bodhisattva:

relying on the threefold *prajñā* and the ten perfections such as giving (*dāna*), they reflect upon and repeatedly hear, contemplate, and cultivate all dharmas—such as the sūtras established and taught by the Buddhas—in accordance with reason within the Mahāyāna; thus, through the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, they constantly engage in contemplative practice.
What merit arises from practicing contemplation based on the three types of wisdom?
It serves to nourish the realms and sense bases, and it leads to the ultimate fulfillment of one's purpose.
If a person practices contemplation based on the wisdom derived from hearing, all their wholesome roots and the nature of their elements will increase.
If one practices contemplation based on the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), it is because the meaning of the names and phrases as they were heard enters the mind and becomes manifest.

If one practices contemplation based on the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), it is because the sought-after objective is accomplished for the purpose of entering the stages (*bhūmi*) and purifying them.
It should be known that this cultivation of contemplation has a companion;
it should be known as being in conjunction with ten kinds of right practices.
It should be known that this practitioner of contemplative cultivation is sustained by these ten kinds of right dharma-practices.
What are the ten kinds of Dharma-practice?
Copying, making offerings, and giving; listening, reading, and upholding;
explaining extensively, reciting, reflecting, and cultivating.

There are ten practices for the cultivation of the Mahāyāna Dharma: first, writing it down; second, making offerings to it; third, giving it to others; fourth, listening with single-minded attention when others recite it; fifth, reading it oneself; sixth, correctly grasping the names, phrases, syllables, and meanings according to reason; seventh, explaining them clearly according to the principles of names, phrases, and syllables; eighth, hearing and reciting it with a correct mind; ninth, reflecting upon it according to reason in a secluded place; and tenth, practicing so that what has entered the mind is not lost.
The immeasurable accumulation of merit consists of these ten kinds of correct practice.
These ten kinds of correct practice possess three types of merit:
first, the path of immeasurable merit; second, the path of the merit of skillful means in practice; and third, the path of pure merit.
Why is it that within the Mahāyāna the Buddha speaks of the most supreme great fruit and retribution, whereas such is not said regarding the dharmas of the Śrāvaka-yāna and so forth?
Why is this so? There are two reasons.
Because it is supremely inexhaustible, and because its benefit for others never ceases.

"Supremely" means that while the sūtras of the Hīnayāna are intended only for self-benefit, the Mahāyāna is equal in its pursuit of both self-benefit and the benefit of others; therefore, it is supreme.

The first is for the sake of one's own benefit, and the second is for the sake of benefiting others; thus there is that which is inferior and that which is superior, and for this reason it is called "victorious.
Great Bodhi is that which reaches the nirvana without remainder.
Regarding the benefit of others, because there is no cessation within the causal stage, it is said to be inexhaustible; being inexhaustible, it surpasses the Lesser Vehicle.
The contemplation and practice have already been explained.
What is practice in accordance with the Dharma?
There are two kinds of practicing in accordance with the Dharma: non-distraction and non-inversion.
Practice in accordance with the Dharma consists of these two types.
First, practice free from distraction; second, practice free from inverted transformation.
Within this context, there are six kinds of distraction; because these six kinds of distraction are eliminated, it is called "free from distraction."
What are the six kinds of distraction? First, distraction of intrinsic nature;
second, distraction of external conditions; third, internal distraction; fourth, distraction of signs; fifth, distraction of coarse afflictions; and sixth, distraction of discursive thought.
Regarding these six types of distraction, what should be understood as their corresponding [antidotes]? Therefore it is said:

Arising of contemplative practice regarding the six sense objects, Craving for flavors, laxity, and restlessness, Lack of resolve toward meditative concentration, And the conceit of "I am" within the sphere of deliberation.
The inferior mind is distracted; the wise should understand this.
Thus, there are six kinds of such conceptual distractions, which a bodhisattva should recognize and abandon.
What are the six types of distraction?
First, arising from meditative concentration into agitation due to the five consciousnesses is called "intrinsic distraction" (*svabhāva-vikṣepa*).
If the mind moves toward the six sense objects, it is called "external distraction" (*bāhya-vikṣepa*).
Craving the flavor of this meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), along with regret, restlessness, and agitation, is called internal distraction.

When the mind has not yet reached certainty or stillness regarding the lower stages, it is called distraction toward signs (*nimitta-vikṣepa*), because one enters meditative absorption by means of those signs.

The conceptualization involving the grasping at a self that arises within meditative concentration is called "coarse distraction," because through this coarse conceptualization, the practice of pride is generated.
Inferior-grade conceptualization is called "conceptual distraction," because it gives rise to the practice of the lower vehicles.
It should be understood that the first two types of distraction prevent what has not yet been attained from being attained; the next two cause what has already been attained to degenerate;
the fifth prevents the attainment of liberation; and the sixth prevents the attainment of unsurpassed enlightenment.
In this regard, one should know that there are ten points of non-erroneousness.
What are these ten? They are:
words, meaning, reflection, the two states of immovability, and the two bases.
Impurity and purity as adventitious, fearlessness and lack of pride—
among these, what dharma is called non-erroneous?
Non-erroneousness is knowledge and vision according to reality and according to measure.
These ten points of non-erroneousness are as follows: first, non-erroneousness regarding names, phrases, and syllables.
As a verse says:
"Because of their accumulation and repeated practice, there are those with meaning and those without meaning."
These words are non-erroneous.
If names, phrases, and syllables are associated with one another, they are called "uninterrupted" and "non-separate" because they are spoken in succession; thus, this entity is its name.
Through repeated practice, names, phrases, and phonemes come to possess meaning;
conversely, if these three are inverted, they lack meaning.
To have such knowledge and vision is called non-erroneousness regarding names, phrases, and phonemes.
What is the non-erroneous nature of objects?
Although they appear as two kinds, they do not exist in the manner they appear;
this is called the non-erroneous nature of objects, which is far removed from the extremes of existence and non-existence.
The manifestation of various objects is twofold:
first, the manifestation of the grasped (*grāhya*), and second, the manifestation of the grasper (*grāhaka*), because they arise as two aspects.
When such non-existence is understood through the insight that objects do not exist in the manner in which they manifest, this is called the non-perversion regarding objects.
How so? This meaning is as follows: it is free from the characteristic of existence because the grasper and the grasped do not exist;
yet it is free from the characteristic of non-existence because there is the presence of the distraction that resembles the grasper and the grasped.
What is non-erroneous reflection?
This refers to verbal permeation and verbal reflection; it relies on non-erroneous reflection to manifest these two kinds of causes.

The words for the grasped and the grasper, as well as the linguistic conceptualizations that have been habituated through perfuming, are the basis for the false discrimination of the grasper and the grasped.
If one gives rise to such knowledge and vision, this is called non-erroneous conceptualization in all respects.
What is reflection? It is that which manifests as the false appearance of the grasper and the grasped.
Because it arises from the two factors of speech and the dharma of names, phrases, and syllables, it serves as the basis for these two factors.
Because this reflection is free from error regarding the object.
What is the non-erroneous state of immovability?
One should know that although things such as illusions do not exist [inherently], they nevertheless possess the sense of being existent.
This is immovable and non-erroneous, because existence and non-existence do not disperse.
This meaning is both existent and non-existent, as has already been explained previously.
This existence and non-existence are, for example, like a magical illusion.

That which is like a magical illusion does not exist as a substantial entity such as an elephant or a horse, yet it is not non-existent; it merely appears as an elephant and so forth because it exists as a mental distraction.
The meaning is likewise: it does not exist as that which is grasped or the grasper, just as it manifests.
It is not that they do not exist; rather, it is because only the appearances of similar, scattered [mental] distractions exist.
The term "and so forth" refers to analogies such as a mirage, a dream, an illusion, and the moon reflected in water.
Such principles should be understood in this way.
Having already perceived the meaning of the analogies such as illusions, the mind does not proceed in a distorted manner; this is called "immovability without inversion.
Because of this non-inverted mind, there is no mental distraction within the state of non-apprehension.
What are the two aspects of non-delusion?
That "everything exists only as names" and that "conceptualization does not arise"—
this is the non-delusion regarding specific characteristics.
All phenomena exist as nothing more than names and expressions.
What are these names?
They are all eyes and forms, up to and including mind and mental objects.
Such knowledge and vision serve as the antidote to all false conceptualizations; therefore, they are called the non-erroneousness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
What, then, is meant by "specific characteristic"?
Is it false or is it real? This characteristic is called "real," and within the specific characteristics of reality, it is non-erroneous. Why is this so?
If it were for the sake of conventional truth, all phenomena would not merely have names; such is the nature of clinging.
What is the non-erroneous universal characteristic?
Beyond the dharma-realm, there is not a single phenomenon that exists.
Therefore, the universal characteristic of the dharmadhātu is that this wisdom is non-erroneous.
There is no separate dharma apart from selflessness that exists as a truly real entity; thus, the dharmadhātu is the universal characteristic of all things, because its essence is equal.
To know and see in this way is called the non-erroneous nature of the universal characteristic.
What is the non-erroneous nature of purity and impurity?
It is the non-extinction and the extinction of inverted and false conceptualization.
This impurity and purity are non-perverted with respect to that [reality].
As long as perversion and improper mental attention persist and have not been exhausted, this is called the impurity of the dharma-realm.
If there is neither non-existence nor exhaustion, this is called the purity of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-viśuddhi*).
If one possesses such knowledge and vision, this is called the non-perversion regarding impurity and purity, respectively.
What is the non-perversion regarding the adventitious?
Because the nature of the dharma-realm is pure, it is likened to space;
these two kinds are adventitious, and this is their non-perversion.
Furthermore, there are the dharma-realm, suchness, reality, and space, which are pure by their very nature.
These two kinds of dharmas are called "adventitious" because they are not original dharmas; they were previously impure and subsequently become pure.
If one possesses such knowledge and vision, this is called the non-erroneous [realization] of adventitious characteristics.
What is the non-erroneous [realization] of being without fear and without pride?
"In both the defiled and the pure, neither person nor phenomena exist."
Because there is no cause, there is neither fear nor pride; these two states are without inversion.
As for the person, there is neither defilement nor purification.
It is the same with phenomena (*dharma*): they were originally without defilement, and later they are without purification.
Why is this so? Because persons and phenomena do not exist substantially, there is not a single thing among these two that belongs to either the pure category or the impure category.
When it is an impure state, there is not a single dharma that undergoes diminution; nor is there any increase when it is a pure state.
At the time of the Chapter on Purity, not a single thing is augmented.
Because these two dharmas give rise to fear and arrogance, if one possesses such knowledge and vision, it is called being without fear, without arrogance, and without inversion.
These ten kinds of non-erroneous [realization] should be established in their respective order within the ten kinds of vajra-bases (*vajrapada*).
What are the ten kinds of vajra-bases? First, the non-erroneous realization of existence and non-existence;

second, the non-erroneous realization of the basis; third, the non-erroneous realization of the analogy of illusion; fourth, the non-erroneous realization of non-conceptuality; fifth, the non-erroneous realization of natural purity; sixth, the non-erroneous realization of impurity; seventh, the non-erroneous realization of purity; eighth, the non-erroneous realization of the analogy of empty space; ninth, the non-erroneous realization of non-decrease; and tenth, the non-erroneous realization of non-increase.
The practice in accordance with the Dharma has already been explained.
What, then, is the practice of avoiding the two extremes?
It is as the Buddha taught the Middle Way of signlessness to Kāśyapa and others in the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*.
What are the two extremes?
To distance oneself from these, this Middle Way should be understood.
The extreme of heterogeneity and the extreme of identity—these are the extremes of the non-Buddhists and the Śrāvakas.
Increase and decrease, the two kinds of persons and dharmas, are not the aids to the antidotes;
the extremes of annihilation and permanence are called "having limits.
Subject and object, as well as defilement and purity, each have two and three [aspects].
The discrimination of the two extremes should be known to be of seven kinds:
existence and non-existence, that which is to be ceased, the cessation of what is fearful and fear itself,
the extremes of the grasper and the grasped, and the matters of correctness and error, as well as existence and non-existence.
Non-arising and simultaneity are the extremes of conceptualizing existence and non-existence.

To establish the self as distinct from the aggregates such as form is one extreme; to establish the self and form as being identical is another extreme. To depart from these two extremes, the Buddha taught the Middle Way: not seeing a self, not seeing a person, not seeing a sentient being, and not seeing a life-sustainer.
Why is this so? If a person clings to the view of a self, they do not escape these two extremes: that the life-principle (*jīva*) is distinct [from the body] and the body is also distinct [from it].
If one does not grasp at such clinging, then the distinctness itself is the life-principle, and the name itself is the body.
These two views definitely exist; this [Middle Way] is the middle path between them, so that these two attachments cannot arise.
That form and so forth are eternal is the extreme of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas); that they are impermanent is the extreme of the Śrāvakas.
To depart from these two extremes, the Buddha taught the Middle Way: because one does not regard form and other phenomena as either permanent or impermanent, this is called the Middle Way.
To assert a self is the exaggeration of the extreme; to deny selflessness is the deprecation of the extreme, for there exists a person who is a conventional designation.

To depart from these two extremes, the Buddha taught the Middle Way: that which is neither "self" nor "non-self," for in the middle between those two there is no duality, as it is free from conceptual discrimination upon contact.
To claim that the mind truly exists is the extreme of superimposition; to claim that it does not exist at all is the extreme of denial.
To avoid these two extremes, the Buddha taught the Middle Way: herein there is no mentation, no mind, no consciousness, and no attention.
All unwholesome dharmas are called the impure category and are not aids to the Path; all wholesome dharmas and so forth constitute the pure category and are termed the side of the antidote.
To depart from these two extremes, the Buddha taught the Middle Way; the Buddha taught that these two kinds of extremes neither go nor come, and are beyond analogy and beyond words.
That which exists is called the person and the phenomena of the extreme of eternalism; that which does not exist is called the person and the phenomena of the extreme of nihilism.
Because one is free from these two extremes, the Buddha taught the Middle Way; this "middle" between the two kinds [of extremes] is what is called the Middle Way, as previously explained.
Ignorance grasps one extreme and can grasp the second extreme;
as it is with ignorance, so it is with knowledge.
All conditioned phenomena grasp one extreme and can grasp the other extreme.
Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are also like this.
Just as with ignorance (*avidyā*), up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), there is that which is grasped (*grāhya*) and that which grasps (*grāhaka*).
The cessation of old age and death is the extreme of the grasped; the [cessation] that grasps is the second extreme.
This path of cessation consists of the grasped and the grasper; these two extremes of the grasped and the grasper are distinguished by their differentiation into the dark and the bright portions.
To avoid these two extremes, the Buddha taught the Middle Way.
The Buddha taught that ignorance (*avidyā*) and clarity (*vidyā*)—these two are non-dual and non-existent—as explained at length in the sūtras.
Why is this so? Because the entities of the grasped and the grasper within ignorance, clarity, and so forth, do not exist.
There are three types of defilement:
first, afflictions; second, karma; and third, the defilement of birth.
Furthermore, the defilement of afflictions is threefold: first, various views; second, the manifestation of desire, hatred, and delusion; and third, the further aspiration for rebirth.

To counteract these three, the Buddha taught the knowledge of the liberation door of emptiness, the knowledge of the liberation door of signlessness, and the knowledge of the liberation door of wishlessness.
Regarding karmic defilement, it consists of the performance of wholesome and unwholesome deeds.
To counteract this karma, the Buddha taught that wisdom is without fabrication.

For those who give rise to defilement, there further arise, in the intermediate state and after birth, the mind and mental factors that arise moment by moment; thus, there is the arising of a continuous succession that is never severed.
To counteract this, the Buddha taught that wisdom is non-arising, wisdom is non-origination, and wisdom is without intrinsic nature.
The elimination of these three kinds of defilement is called purification.
Knowing emptiness and so forth, as well as the defiled emptiness and so forth, is called the purity of the object (*ālambana-viśuddhi*).
Furthermore, all antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) are called the purity of practice (*caryā-viśuddhi*).
Because of this practice, afflictions are eliminated and do not arise again; this is called the purity of the fruit (*phala-viśuddhi*).

These three kinds of purity—the emptiness of defilement and so forth—are like the three kinds of emptiness resulting from purification and so forth, because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena does not exist and because the intrinsic nature of the dharma-realm is without differentiation.
Furthermore, there are dharmas such as wisdom and emptiness, which are neither produced by defilement nor produced by knowledge.
Why is this? It is because these dharmas, such as emptiness and so forth, exist by way of their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is free from defilement, if one conceives of and discriminates the dharma-realm as being sometimes defiled and sometimes pure, this constitutes an extreme. Since the self-nature of phenomena is inherently undefiled and lacks both defilement and purity, such a grasping becomes an extreme.

To distance oneself from these extremes, the Buddha taught this Middle Way: it is not that emptiness is produced by non-duality to make all phenomena empty; rather, all phenomena are empty of their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
These points are explained in detail in the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*.
Furthermore, there are seven kinds of conceptualization regarding the two extremes. What are the seven?
First, conceptualizing one extreme within existence; second, conceptualizing one extreme within non-existence.
There is a person who is [conceived as] real; in order to extinguish this notion, emptiness is established.
There is a selflessness that is [conceived as] real; in order to extinguish this notion, non-emptiness is established.
Based on these two types of conceptualization, there arise the attachments to existence and non-existence.
To depart from these two extremes, the Buddha taught the Middle Way.
That which is empty does not annihilate the person and so forth.
What is it for? It is for nothing, because all phenomena are of a spontaneous nature, as explained at length in the sutra.

All afflictions such as ignorance should be ceased and extinguished, while dharmas such as clarity should be produced through the Path, which is capable of bringing about their cessation and extinction.
Because such conceptualizations regarding that which is to be ceased and that which can cease [give rise to fear], one experiences dread toward emptiness.
To eliminate these two extremes of conceptualization, the Buddha taught the analogies of emptiness.

To conceptualize what is fearful is one extreme; to become terrified because of that which is fearful is another extreme. To conceptualize the objects of the senses, such as forms and so forth, and thereby give rise to fear and the fear of suffering, is likewise an extreme.
To eliminate these two kinds of conceptual extremes regarding fear, the Buddha taught the analogy of the painter.
The previous analogy was spoken in reference to followers of the Hīnayāna; the present analogy is spoken in reference to Bodhisattvas.
The conceptualization of the apprehended object is one extreme, and the conceptualization of the apprehending subject is another extreme.
To avoid these two extremes, the Buddha taught the analogy of the magician. Why is this so?
The wisdom of consciousness-only produces the wisdom of the absence of objects.
Regarding the wisdom of the absence of objects: it eliminates the wisdom of consciousness-only.
Because objects have no substantial reality, consciousness also does not arise.
In this context, the discrimination of what is similar constitutes one side of the correct position (*samyak-sthāna*), while the discrimination of what is erroneous constitutes the other side.
One discriminates the vision of reality as the correct position and [the vision of] error as the incorrect position.
To depart from these two extremes, the Buddha taught the analogy of fire produced by rubbing two pieces of wood together.
For example, although the two pieces of wood do not possess the characteristic of fire, fire arises from them; once the fire has arisen, it returns to burn those very two pieces of wood.
Thus, the characteristic of the non-abiding state and the characteristic of the abiding state have the true vision of correct thorough penetration as their mark.
Once the faculty of noble wisdom has arisen and been perfected, this is the mark of the true vision of the abiding state.

Furthermore, there is cessation and extinction; herein, the analogy corresponds to this: in the true vision, the characteristics of the state of error do not exist, nor do the characteristics of the state of error exist [as such], for even the state of error is absent, as it conforms to the state of reality.
There is one side of conceptualization regarding the existence of objects, and one side of conceptualization regarding the non-existence of objects.
Regarding the existence of objects, there is first the conceptualization of mental attention (*manasikāra*) through wisdom, followed by the conceptualization of effortlessness (*anābhoga*).
To avoid these two extremes regarding merit, the Buddha taught the analogy of the lamp’s light.
To conceptualize the non-arising of one side is to conceptualize the equality of time as another side.
If one conceptualizes the non-arising of the path of antidotes, one conceptualizes the long duration of afflictions.
To depart from these two extremes, the Buddha taught the second analogy of the lamp.
Having already explained the practice that departs from the fourteen pairs of extremes,
what is the practice of the "superior existence" and so forth?
One should know that the practice of excellence and so forth pertains to the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
What is the practice of excellence and so forth?
Within the ten stages, whichever *pāramitā* is supreme and peerless at any given stage is called the "practice of excellence."
If all places are identical and without distinction, this is called "equal cultivation.
The unsurpassed cultivation has already been explained.
What is the unsurpassed objective sphere?
One should know the establishment and the nature-realm, the accomplished and the means of accomplishment,
the support of certainty, penetration and vastness,
conduct and the realm of birth, as well as the supreme and so forth.
Such objective spheres are twelvefold. What are the twelve? First, the sphere of establishing the designation of phenomena;

second, the sphere of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); third, the sphere of that which is accomplished; fourth, the sphere of the means of accomplishment; fifth, the sphere of maintenance; sixth, the sphere of decisive maintenance; seventh, the sphere of fixed reliance; eighth, the sphere of thorough penetration; ninth, the sphere of continuity; tenth, the sphere of superior attainment; eleventh, the sphere of birth; and twelfth, the sphere of supreme excellence.
Among these, the first refers to the various dharmas such as the pāramitās, as established by the Buddha.
The second is the dharma-tathatā (suchness).

The third and fourth follow the sequence mentioned previously: because of the thorough penetration of the dharma-dhātu and because of the attainment of the practice of the pāramitās and other dharmas.
The fifth is the sphere of wisdom derived from hearing;
the sixth is the sphere of wisdom derived from reflection.
What is meant by "decisive retention"?
Because it is already known that this dharma can be maintained;
the seventh is the sphere of wisdom cultivated through meditation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), because it is maintained by relying on the internal basis (*adhyātma-āśraya*);
the eighth is the sphere of vision within the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*).
The ninth is the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) up through the seventh ground.
The tenth consists of the mundane and supramundane paths within those seven grounds, because it brings about the accomplishment of all phenomena according to their categories (*prakāra*).
The eleventh is within the eighth stage;

the twelfth is within the three stages beginning with the ninth. These constitute the first and second spheres of experience, which are the spheres of equality throughout each respective stage as previously described.
Regarding the remaining objects (*viṣaya*), these are the distinctions manifested by the preceding two.
The objects have already been explained.
What, then, is their cultivation and arising?
Endowment and non-destruction, avoidance and fulfillment,
arising and firmness, non-abiding according to circumstances,
non-obstruction and non-abandonment— these ten should be known as the arisings of practice.
There are ten types of such cultivation and arising.
Among these, the fulfillment of causes and conditions is called "cultivation and arising of nature.
Not slandering the Mahāyāna teachings is called "cultivation and arising of aspiration and joy."
Avoiding the vehicles of the Hīnayāna is called the cultivation of the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*).
Perfecting the practice of the *pāramitās* is called the cultivation of spiritual practice (*pratipatti*).
Giving rise to the Noble Path is called the cultivation of entering the stage of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Because firm roots of goodness have been cultivated over a long period of time, it is called the "arising of the habituation of maturing sentient beings.
Because the mind achieves accomplishment in accordance with its objects, it is called the "arising of the habituation of the pure land."

Not abiding within either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa, one attains the prediction of the stage of non-retrogression; because one does not fall back into saṃsāra or nirvāṇa, all hindrances are extinguished, which is termed the arising of the Buddha-ground habituation.
Not abandoning these matters is called the manifestation of the bodhisattva’s practice.
Thus, this treatise is titled "Discrimination between the Middle and the Extremes" (*Madhyāntavibhāga*), because it brings about a thorough understanding of the Middle Way.
Furthermore, because there is discrimination between the middle way and the two extremes, and because these two extremes can manifest therein;
one remains detached from both ends—beginning and end—and does not cling to these two points, as they are manifested through discrimination in accordance with reality.
Therefore, it is titled the *Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra* (Treatise on the Discrimination of the Middle and the Extremes). This treatise discriminates the middle, the profound and true meaning,
the great meaning, and all meanings, thereby removing all inauspiciousness.
Regarding this, the *Madhyāntavibhāga* (Discrimination of the Middle and the Extremes) has its name and meaning as previously explained.
Its meaning is profoundly secret because it is not within the sphere of discursive thought (*vitarka*) or investigation (*vicāra*).
Its meaning is truly firm because it cannot be refuted by any other doctrines.
Because it is the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi, it is of great significance;
because its purpose is the welfare of both oneself and others, it is of all purposes.
Since the meanings of the three vehicles are manifested through this treatise, it is able to eliminate all inauspiciousness.

Regarding "inauspiciousness": it refers to the three grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) and the three grades of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). Because [this practice] can eliminate and extinguish this inauspiciousness of birth-and-death and afflictions;
because it can destroy the obstacles to the four virtues and can sustain and uphold those four virtues, it is said to "remove inauspiciousness."
Regarding the supreme multitudes of meanings, briefly stated, there are three kinds of supremacy:
first, correct practice; second, correct support; and third, the fruit of correct practice.
This cultivation is as previously explained: being incomparable in its categories, its skillful means, and its contemplation of the various dharmas established by the Buddha within the Mahāyāna.
According to the principle, there is no distraction and no error: if one cultivates śamatha, there is no distraction; if one cultivates vipaśyanā, there is no erroneous transformation.
It acts as it does for the sake of renunciation, because it accords with the Middle Way.
It abides within the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and practices superior forms of existence and so forth.
Regarding the non-erroneous manifold meanings, this is because names and phrases are non-erroneous.
He penetrates the characteristics of meditative concentration because his understanding of their meaning is non-erroneous;

he penetrates the characteristics of wisdom because his contemplation is non-erroneous, because he has attained freedom from the causes and conditions of error, and because there is no distraction or inversion.
In this regard, the characteristics of the Middle Way are clearly attained, which brings about the accomplishment of the non-erroneous specific characteristics.
Based on this, one gives rise to the remedy and attains the path that discerns saṃsāra.
Because there is no inversion regarding the common characteristics, one attains penetration into the pure factors (*śukla-pakṣa*).
Because there is no inversion regarding the intrinsic impurity and purity [of the factors], there is the non-cessation and cessation of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Because there is no inversion regarding the respective attainments of knowledge, one perceives impurity and purity as they truly are.
Because it is free from fear, free from arrogance, and free from error, it eliminates all obstacles and brings about liberation.
It is the single path to emptiness and nirvāṇa, illuminated by the light of the Buddha’s solar speech;
though the conduct of the noble assembly is fully matured, the blind cannot see it.
Having already understood the Buddha’s true teaching, know that life hangs by a thread;
while the power of the various afflictions is still strong, seek the Way and do not be negligent.
Herein ends the "Supreme Vehicle Chapter" of the *Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra*.
Composed by the Mahāyāna practitioner Vasubandhu Śākyabhikṣu.
Now I have composed this treatise for the sake of merit, wisdom, and practice in the world,
so that all beings everywhere may attain Bodhi according to their wishes.
